# The Calling Of Saint Rocky

January 1, 2026 January 1, 2026[Rihn & Curcio](https://www.thefightcity.com/author/movies/ "Rihn & Curcio")

The series began with [The Prizefighter And The Lady](https://www.thefightcity.com/max-baer-prizefighter-and-the-lady-boxing/), and then it continued with [Requiem For A Heavyweight](https://www.thefightcity.com/rihn-curcio-requiem-for-a-heavyweight-boxing-cinema/). Now writers David Curcio and Andrew Rihn turn their insightful gazes to a fight film which, arguably, has had more impact on both boxing and the larger culture than any other. No one could have foreseen the incredible success of _Rocky_ when it was released in 1976, but it went on to win Best Picture at the Academy Awards and turned Sylvester Stallone into a Hollywood star, before launching a franchise which generated hundreds of millions in box office revenue.

![Image 3: Rocky movie ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-poster-image.jpeg)

But if the sequels that followed the Oscar-winning original devolved into orgies of kitsch and cliché, the film that spawned them was something else entirely, a thoughtful and moving work, not to mention an arresting slice of urban Americana, whose intriguing themes and subtleties have, for some at least, become obscured by time. So let’s revisit _Rocky_ and let our thoughtful scribes renew our appreciation for what is surely the most successful and influential of fight films.Check it out:

**David Curcio:**Andrew, I know you’ve viewed _Rocky_ many more times than I have and I’m betting you will have noticed an image in the opening scene I found striking, that being a large portrait of Christ over the boxing ring.

**Andrew Rihn:**No matter how many times I watch _Rocky_, and I’ve watched it a lot, that opening shot always surprises me. Christ is holding the Eucharist and the camera then slowly tilts down to reveal the ring, where Rocky and Spider Rico are slugging it out. It’s a club fight and the cinematographer has lit the scene like a George Bellows painting. The ring action is rough and the audience is gambling and looking for blood. It’s a seedy environment. I suspect we’re to appreciate the apparent duality of the holiness and the unholiness. And I take it as a reminder that seedy joints like this are, according to the Gospels, exactly the kind of place where Jesus hung out. When Christ was criticized for fraternizing with his disciples and other riff raff, he shrugged it off. “I came not to call the righteous,” he says, “but sinners to repentance.” And this is not the only time we see a religious image in the film. In his apartment, Rocky has a print of Caravaggio’s _The Calling of St. Matthew._

![Image 4](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Rocky-and-Spider.jpg)

Opening scene: Rocky defeats Spider Rico at the Resurrection Athletic Club.

**D.C.** Which is notable considering that Matthew also hung out in some of the sleaziest joints around before he was called. But in fact the poster in Rocky’s apartment is a riff on the painting titled “The Minstrels,” in which the faces of The Beatles are super-imposed. Still, its pertinent in that Matthew was, like Rocky, a small-time hood, so to speak. Tax-collectors were known for being crooked, while Rocky is also a collector, in his case a leg-breaker for a “cheap, second-rate loan shark,” as Mickey calls him.

**A.R.** It was controversial to say the Beatles were more popular than Jesus, but here they are certainly bigger than Matthew. I love that Rocky’s poster is this kind of pop culture palimpsest. The religious allusion is there, but delivered by non-religious figures. It also dovetails with Rocky’s sense of humor, his goofy charm, continually cracking bad jokes and corny lines.

**D.C.** Maybe the beauty here is that Rocky, as a character, stays agnostic throughout. God is present in the crosses, paintings, and even parody prints, but he’s never directly mentioned, which leaves it open-ended in the best way. But the religious imagery is important. And we recall how in _Rocky II_ he makes a special trip to go and ask for a blessing from Father Carmine before battling Apollo Creed again.

![Image 5: Rocky and Gazzo](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-Gazzo.jpg)

Rocky with his boss, loan shark Tony Gazzo.

**A.R.** Interestingly, Caravaggio’s masterpiece is a favorite painting of Pope Francis. He has said he sees himself in the stunned, disbelieving faces. “The calling of Matthew reminds us that when Christ makes us his disciples, he does not look to our past but to the future.” That’s definitely a theme in the movie. Does our past determine our future? We see this with Paulie, with Adrian, and in the arguments between Rocky and Mickey.

**D.C.** Character development in _Rocky_ is extraordinary when one considers how the film is so rooted in the present. This is driven home by the family pictures on Rocky’s mirror, for which no explanation is offered, as well as Paulie and Adrian’s toxic codependency and perpetual inertia. Also Mickey’s past as a legit but forgotten fighter. References to these histories are scant and we can only access these lives in the present. Further, these three characters, along with the loan shark, Tony Gazzo, comprise the whole of Rocky’s life in love and work. The former manifests in his affair with Adrian; the latter in his desire to quit collecting as a petty thug, to be something more. Rocky’s no hood, a point driven home by his love of animals, when he talks to the birds in the pet shop like he’s Saint Francis preaching to the sparrows. But while Adrian is the flame that fires up his heart, Mickey is the one to grab Rocky by the scruff. His first words in the film—”Shut up!”—set the tone for a muddled relationship: Rocky, the prodigal son who’s disappointed the old man a few too many times, and Mickey, the absent father with whom it may be too late to make amends.

![Image 6: Rocky in his apartment ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-apartment-calling-small.jpg)

Rocky and “The Minstrels.”

**A.R.** It’s interesting how much _Rocky_ gets misremembered, largely because of [the numerous sequels](https://www.thefightcity.com/creed-ii-movie-boxing/), which are completely different films in terms of tone and depth. As a result, it seems we only remember the clichés, the caricatures. What strikes me when I re-watch _Rocky_ is that he isn’t “called” by Apollo until about halfway through. A full fifty-percent of the movie is just scene setting and character building. It’s a very 1970s pace for filmmaking, comparable to others of the same year like _Taxi Driver_ and _Marathon Man_. And when Rocky is finally “called,” remember, it isn’t because of his worthiness. Creed picks his name out of a book because he likes the rhyme of “Italian Stallion.” Rocky is a self-described “ham and egger.” He isn’t deserving and he knows it and he initially turns down the offer. We never see him agree to the fight on camera and a jump cut to the press conference confirms it’s happening. Likewise, we never hear the conversation where Rocky and Mickey agree to work together. They shout and argue and plead, but when they finally put aside the anger and bitterness in the dark of a nighttime Philadelphia street, the microphone goes silent.

**D.C.** Since you bring them up, I have to note that in terms of opening credit sequences, _Rocky_ is almost identical in style to _Taxi Driver_ and _Marathon Man_. Now Rocky’s worthiness as a challenger, or lack thereof, is an important element in the film’s pathos, but you’re right in that his doubts lie less with his ability to take on the champ—after all, he believes he has the ability to be a good sparring partner for Creed—than with his dignity and merit, and it’s that desire to make himself matter, to prove that he’s not “just another bum,” that elevates the film. That and the fact that the movie works as a powerful love story. These elements cohere so well that it’s impossible to tune out halfway through just because the plot takes its abundant liberties with the realities of the sport. In fact, the fight seems almost incidental, a bonus, when weighed against the love story. I imagine that element brought in more female viewers and likely helped it to earn the accolades it received.

![Image 7: Rocky and Adrian ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Adrian-and-Rocky-pet-shop.jpg)

Adrian and Rocky in the pet store.

**A.R.** I agree and I think _Rocky_ gets a bum rap as being this very generic, commercial pandering type of film, but it really is a good example of what is sometimes called “American New Wave” filmmaking, a style that dominated in the seventies. That’s what gives it a similar feel to pictures like _Marathon Man_ and _Taxi Driver_. There was a lot of cinematic innovation going on, and _Rocky_ was no exception. It was one of the first pictures to feature the newly-invented Steadicam, for instance. A number of the iconic _Rocky_ shots would not have been possible without that technology. Rocky running up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, for example, would have looked completely different without it. Now we’ve mentioned Mickey, Adrian, Paulie, and Apollo, and the movie couldn’t be what it is without that supporting cast. Do you have a favorite?

**D.C.** To me, Paulie is the most captivating. Like the others, his backstory is unknown, though that’s rectified in the sequels. He may seem like the least consequential of the five major characters, but without him, the story would be so tightly composed as to implode on itself. It’s interesting that Stallone originally wanted Harvey Keitel to take the role, though I think he would have been far too domineering: his mien, his physique, and his methodology are ill-suited to a loser like Paulie.

**A.R.** I think Burt Young was perfectly cast. He does this subtle gesture, puffing out his lower lip whenever he takes a nip from his bottle. It’s so perfectly infantile and pathetic. I would have given him the Academy Award for that alone.

![Image 8](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Paulie-beer.jpg)

Burt Young as Paulie.

**D.C.** Paulie plays like the Jungian shadow to both Rocky and his sister. His penchant for violence reverberates as much as Rocky’s attempt to escape it. This is most evident in his wish to work for Gazzo. As he says, “Breakin’ bones don’t bother me.” Anyone who saw 1974’s _The Gambler_ knows he’s well versed in that department. While his sister works in a pet shop nurturing innocent souls waiting to be rescued, sort of like the rest of the characters, Paulie spends his days swinging dead cow carcasses. The sibling relationship keeps him in a perpetual state of arrested development in which he figures so long as he’s taking care of his sister, he doesn’t have to move on with his own life. That’s why it causes him such distress when Adrian comes to develop her own volition. As siblings, they’re such opposites that Adrian’s mousiness is buried under Paulie’s wrath and domination. But she’s just as intriguing.

**A.R.** It’s interesting to consider Adrian in the context of past boxing movies as nearly all of them treat women as plot devices rather than full characters. A trope in boxing movies was giving the protagonist two love interests, the nice girl-next-door who knew him before he was famous, and then later, a gold-digging femme fatale. He then had to choose: be true to his core values or sell out to a life of fame and riches. _Rocky_ takes a different path, with Stallone’s character staying true to one woman.The movie, and the series as a whole, gets some flak for leaving Adrian undeveloped, but I think that looking at her in context reveals some layers that are easy to overlook.

![Image 9: Adrian and Rocky ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Adrian-and-Rocky-go-skating.jpeg)

Adrian and Rocky on their first date.

She begins the movie coupled to her brother Paulie, who feels chronically disrespected and needs Adrian’s near-total dependency to satisfy his own ego, to feel like he matters. Maybe he’s compensating for some lack of control in his life, but if Adrian is underwritten, it is here: the hows and whys that go unanswered in regards to tolerating her brother’s behavior for so long. If she yearns for something more, we come to understand it only through Rocky. But Paulie interprets Adrian’s independence as a threat and he lashes out at the couple that he helped to create. Adrian’s dramatic break with her brother —”What do I owe you?!”— is a powerful moment from a quiet character and I think one can see Adrian’s defiance of Paulie in 1976 as a meaningful feminist act.

**D.C.** Which only makes the movie’s love story that much more powerful, doesn’t it. It’s not just about two people falling in love, but about how that love transforms them, gives them new life. With Rocky’s help, Adrian breaks out of her shell and asserts herself, while it’s her love that gives Rocky the strength to suffer everything he must go through to give Apollo Creed the fight of his life, to “go the distance.” As I say, it’s the love story that makes the movie something more than the sum of its parts.

![Image 10: Rocky and Paulie ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-and-Paulie.jpg)

Rocky and Paulie at the meat packing plant.

**A.R.** Yeah, the suffering of Rocky. That’s an important theme, isn’t it? And it brings us back to Christ and the Biblical allusions. Rocky is called but then, like so many saints and followers of Christ, he has to withstand what amounts to torture. The exaggerated violence and bloodiness of the fight scene, with Rocky enduring almost obscene punishment, his face a mass of welts before he begs Mickey to cut him with a razor, it’s all meant to function as something more than just gratuitous carnage.

**D.C.** And of course the pathos of that reflects how the movie has worked so hard to make Rocky such an endearing character, a sort of gentle giant with a heart of gold. Early in the film he encounters a barely conscious drunk lying on the pavement. He doesn’t step over him or walk past, but heaves the poor guy over his shoulder and carries him into the bar. Later he counsels a young girl, Marie, and even walks her home. She rejects his advice and calls him a “creepo,” but we see Rocky’s heart is always in the right place, that he cares. And so the viewer cares about him when he’s getting beaten to a pulp and pounded all over the ring.

**A.R.** Yeah, an intriguing, if minor, development in the sequels is when Stallone resurrects the character of Marie in _Rocky Balboa_, and Rocky works that goofy, bad joke charm thing again, like with Adrian in the pet store. Reportedly, there was serious consideration given to a Marie and Rocky romance for that film before Stallone and company, thankfully, rejected the idea.

**D.C.** Shifting gears, let’s talk about Rocky’s apartment. It’s the only hint the viewer has into his past which, for a film that remains completely rooted in the present, is virtually nil. We can tell he’s Catholic as evinced by the crucifixes on his walls, but I know you have other observations worth parsing out.

![Image 11](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/rocky-balboa-american-photos-mirror.jpg)

“… Christ does not look to our past but to the future.”

**A.R.** I love the set dressing that went into the apartment. It’s where much of the movie takes place and it’s a set we won’t see again in the Rocky series. A bachelor pad in extremus, it’s heaped with detritus, nearly decomposing. The walls are dirty, damaged. It’s a reflection of how Rocky is living at the time, of how his bad habits have become ingrained behaviors, or what Mickey calls “a waste of life.” Rocky stuffs beer bottles between the couch cushions. There’s no screen on the screen door. When he pulls ice out of his freezer, he drops a few ice cubes and doesn’t bother to pick them up. When Mickey drops in, Rocky throws darts into his bathroom door. Thankfully, we’re spared the sight of his bathroom. As you mentioned, there’s an obvious hint at the past in a set of photos tucked into the side of a mirror, real photos from Stallone’s childhood. Next to the mirror, knives are stabbed into the wall, U.S. military trench knives, in fact, an M1917 and a Mark I. Rocky hangs that famous black fedora on the Mark I. There’s a mattress tied around a pole, apparently a makeshift punching bag, with a giant buck knife sticking out of it. And when Rocky enters his apartment with Adrian for the first time, he hangs his coat on the handle of a machete stabbed into the wall. The knives speak to the violence that permeates Rocky’s world, but they also reveal his character. He isn’t wielding these knives as weapons but using them as hat racks. It suggests that while Rocky is in that world of violence and depravity, he isn’t _of_ that world, to paraphrase St. Paul.

**D.C.** Another prominent detail in the apartment, the portrait of [Rocky Marciano](https://www.thefightcity.com/rocky-marciano-floyd-boxing/), which brings us to Rocky’s name. According to Stallone, “The Brockton Blockbuster” was the sole inspiration for the character, though it seems to me Marciano is one of several facets that comprise the iconic moniker. In fact, Rocky’s hard-scrabble beginnings are closer to [Rocky Graziano’s](https://www.thefightcity.com/july-16-1947-zale-vs-graziano-ii-boxing-legendary/), whose birth name of Barbella, Stallone’s mother’s maiden name, collates neatly with Rocky’s surname, Balboa.

![Image 12](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Apollo-and-Rocky-prefight.jpg)

Carl Weathers as champion Apollo Creed.

**A.R.** And Graziano got his own biopic, _Somebody Up There Likes Me_ (1956), which helped launch the young Paul Newman’s career, much as _Rocky_ launched Stallone’s.

**D.C.** As to Rocky’s fighting moniker, “The Italian Stallion,” it was also used by a 1970s and 80s heavyweight and actor Lee Canalito, though it’s unclear as to who borrowed from whom, since the actors had worked together the previous year. Finally, “Stallone,” Italian for “stallion,” completes the colossal mash-up. When a reporter asks the fictional fighter how he came up with the sobriquet, Rocky responds that he “made that up one night while [he] was eating dinner.” Not likely.

The most obvious avatar is, of course, Chuck Wepner. But Stallone has never acknowledged it. Here I should point out that perfunctory internet searches will pull up quotes and listicles to the contrary, but I’m sticking with Wepner’s story. Was it a coincidence that the Ali vs Wepner bout took place on October 30, 1974, just a week or so before Stallone claims to have penned his script? Wepner even filed a lawsuit for “promotion of the Rocky movies… without consent and without compensation,” grumbling later that the settlement didn’t bring in “a minute percentage” of the fifteen million he wanted. While we’re on the topic of money, it’s worth remembering that Stallone had to forgo payment for his script and his acting in order to get the producers, Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff (who went on to produce [_Raging Bull_](https://www.thefightcity.com/raging-bull-jake-lamotta-film-memoir-boxing/) four years later) to make the film. But he earned $2.5 million from his percentage of box office takes, so he made out just fine.

![Image 13](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/rocky_2_stallone-and-mickey.jpg)

Burgess Meredith as trainer Mickey Goldmill.

**A.R.** It’s interesting to think about the context of Rocky’s release. Not a lot of on-screen characters were talking about the sport of boxing the way Stallone was. From 1949’s _The Set-Up_, to 1962’s [_Requiem for a Heavyweight_](https://www.thefightcity.com/rihn-curcio-requiem-for-a-heavyweight-boxing-cinema/), all the way to 1972’s [_Fat City_](https://www.thefightcity.com/the-edge-of-fat-city/), big-screen boxing was portrayed as pretty bleak. But _Rocky_ was a movie about holding onto hope and finding meaning in the ring, and Stallone was rewarded for that take. He was nominated for two Academy Awards: Best Screenplay and Best Actor, a rare combination of which Stallone was only the third to achieve, after Orson Welles and Charlie Chaplin. Not bad company for a guy who calls himself an “intellectual caveman.”

In all, _Rocky_ was nominated for ten Oscars, including nominations for Stallone, Talia Shire, Burt Young, and Burgess Meredith. It won three, Best Picture, Best Director and Best Film Editing, in a fairly stacked year, going up against _Taxi Driver_, _All the President’s Men_, _Network_, _Marathon Man_, and others. And here’s an interesting fact: _Rocky_ was the first sports movie to win Best Picture, but _not_ the first boxing movie, if we count _On The Waterfront_ (1954) as a boxing picture, which I do. And a boxing movie would not win Best Picture again until 2004’s _Million Dollar Baby_.

**D.C.** I’m a bit puzzled by Stallone’s attribution to [Muhammad Ali](https://www.thefightcity.com/top-12-reasons-muhammad-ali-forever-the-greatest-cassius-clay-joe-frazier-george-foreman-boxing/) as the inspiration for Apollo Creed, who espouses American pride at every turn, even entering the ring dressed as Uncle Sam in a two-dimensional model of the Durham boat. Such patriotism is at odds with Ali’s real-life, anti-American stances, his commitment to the Nation of Islam, and the separatist ideals that he espoused to Alex Haley in their _Playboy_ interviews. All of which is to say that I see no correlation between the real and fictional fighters.

![Image 14](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-vs-Apollo.jpg)

Rocky goes the distance.

**A.R.** That’s interesting because Ali recognized himself in Creed, the boastful Black champion who loves holding court with the press. “Starring Apollo Creed as Muhammad Ali,” he told Roger Ebert when the two watched _Rocky II_ together. And Ali was quick to analyze the success of _Rocky_: “I have been so great in boxing they had to create an image like Rocky, a white image on the screen, to counteract my image in the ring.”

**D.C.** The legacy of Ali has shifted in the past forty years from controversial, oft-despised provocateur, to brave “conscientious objector” and Civil Rights champion. Do you think this has affected the film’s legacy?

**A.R.** There’s no denying _Rocky’s_ cultural legacy, unmatched by any other boxing picture. How ubiquitous is that theme music? Or the phrase “Yo, Adriaaannnn”? For me, re-watching _Rocky_ never fails to yield something new. Sometimes it’s how Stallone refashions the tropes common to pre-Rocky boxing movies: the rise to the championship, the love interest, the influence of organized crime, even the training montage. Rather than avoid these shop-worn clichés, Rocky leans into their legacy, giving each a little twist, creating characters and storylines that feel at once both familiar and original. Other times, it’s noticing and appreciating the little things. How Rocky dresses his [Marciano](https://www.thefightcity.com/sept-23-1952-marciano-vs-walcott-joe-louis-rocky-marciano-jersey-joe-walcott-heavyweight-boxing/) portrait as Santa Claus. Or how after the big fight, Paulie distracts security so Adrian can slip into the ring. Or the morning zoo radio program that plays over the otherwise silent “raw eggs for breakfast” scene.

![Image 15](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-1-poster-steps.jpg)

Holding onto hope: Stallone’s uplifting take was a box office smash.

But perhaps what makes _Rocky_ so perennially relatable is that it’s ultimately about the nobility of the struggle and not the achievement. I think its final genius is that Rocky fights his heart out, but fails to win. I have watched it a hundred times and still I forget this, my memory buoyed or blurred by the cartoonish sequels and that triumphant theme music. But Rocky loses by split decision. And he doesn’t care. After all the training, the heartache, the pressure, all building towards this great struggle, Rocky discovers his apogee is elsewhere. Apollo can have his shiny belt; Rocky has won something more. Like the saints and martyrs of old, Rocky gains the greater victory through suffering and blood, through answering the call and having the courage to fight against the odds._**—****Andrew Rihn & David Curcio**_

# The Calling Of Saint Rocky

January 1, 2026 January 1, 2026[Rihn & Curcio](https://www.thefightcity.com/author/movies/ "Rihn & Curcio")

The series began with [The Prizefighter And The Lady](https://www.thefightcity.com/max-baer-prizefighter-and-the-lady-boxing/), and then it continued with [Requiem For A Heavyweight](https://www.thefightcity.com/rihn-curcio-requiem-for-a-heavyweight-boxing-cinema/). Now writers David Curcio and Andrew Rihn turn their insightful gazes to a fight film which, arguably, has had more impact on both boxing and the larger culture than any other. No one could have foreseen the incredible success of _Rocky_ when it was released in 1976, but it went on to win Best Picture at the Academy Awards and turned Sylvester Stallone into a Hollywood star, before launching a franchise which generated hundreds of millions in box office revenue.

![Image 3: Rocky movie ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-poster-image.jpeg)

But if the sequels that followed the Oscar-winning original devolved into orgies of kitsch and cliché, the film that spawned them was something else entirely, a thoughtful and moving work, not to mention an arresting slice of urban Americana, whose intriguing themes and subtleties have, for some at least, become obscured by time. So let’s revisit _Rocky_ and let our thoughtful scribes renew our appreciation for what is surely the most successful and influential of fight films.Check it out:

**David Curcio:**Andrew, I know you’ve viewed _Rocky_ many more times than I have and I’m betting you will have noticed an image in the opening scene I found striking, that being a large portrait of Christ over the boxing ring.

**Andrew Rihn:**No matter how many times I watch _Rocky_, and I’ve watched it a lot, that opening shot always surprises me. Christ is holding the Eucharist and the camera then slowly tilts down to reveal the ring, where Rocky and Spider Rico are slugging it out. It’s a club fight and the cinematographer has lit the scene like a George Bellows painting. The ring action is rough and the audience is gambling and looking for blood. It’s a seedy environment. I suspect we’re to appreciate the apparent duality of the holiness and the unholiness. And I take it as a reminder that seedy joints like this are, according to the Gospels, exactly the kind of place where Jesus hung out. When Christ was criticized for fraternizing with his disciples and other riff raff, he shrugged it off. “I came not to call the righteous,” he says, “but sinners to repentance.” And this is not the only time we see a religious image in the film. In his apartment, Rocky has a print of Caravaggio’s _The Calling of St. Matthew._

![Image 4](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Rocky-and-Spider.jpg)

Opening scene: Rocky defeats Spider Rico at the Resurrection Athletic Club.

**D.C.** Which is notable considering that Matthew also hung out in some of the sleaziest joints around before he was called. But in fact the poster in Rocky’s apartment is a riff on the painting titled “The Minstrels,” in which the faces of The Beatles are super-imposed. Still, its pertinent in that Matthew was, like Rocky, a small-time hood, so to speak. Tax-collectors were known for being crooked, while Rocky is also a collector, in his case a leg-breaker for a “cheap, second-rate loan shark,” as Mickey calls him.

**A.R.** It was controversial to say the Beatles were more popular than Jesus, but here they are certainly bigger than Matthew. I love that Rocky’s poster is this kind of pop culture palimpsest. The religious allusion is there, but delivered by non-religious figures. It also dovetails with Rocky’s sense of humor, his goofy charm, continually cracking bad jokes and corny lines.

**D.C.** Maybe the beauty here is that Rocky, as a character, stays agnostic throughout. God is present in the crosses, paintings, and even parody prints, but he’s never directly mentioned, which leaves it open-ended in the best way. But the religious imagery is important. And we recall how in _Rocky II_ he makes a special trip to go and ask for a blessing from Father Carmine before battling Apollo Creed again.

![Image 5: Rocky and Gazzo](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-Gazzo.jpg)

Rocky with his boss, loan shark Tony Gazzo.

**A.R.** Interestingly, Caravaggio’s masterpiece is a favorite painting of Pope Francis. He has said he sees himself in the stunned, disbelieving faces. “The calling of Matthew reminds us that when Christ makes us his disciples, he does not look to our past but to the future.” That’s definitely a theme in the movie. Does our past determine our future? We see this with Paulie, with Adrian, and in the arguments between Rocky and Mickey.

**D.C.** Character development in _Rocky_ is extraordinary when one considers how the film is so rooted in the present. This is driven home by the family pictures on Rocky’s mirror, for which no explanation is offered, as well as Paulie and Adrian’s toxic codependency and perpetual inertia. Also Mickey’s past as a legit but forgotten fighter. References to these histories are scant and we can only access these lives in the present. Further, these three characters, along with the loan shark, Tony Gazzo, comprise the whole of Rocky’s life in love and work. The former manifests in his affair with Adrian; the latter in his desire to quit collecting as a petty thug, to be something more. Rocky’s no hood, a point driven home by his love of animals, when he talks to the birds in the pet shop like he’s Saint Francis preaching to the sparrows. But while Adrian is the flame that fires up his heart, Mickey is the one to grab Rocky by the scruff. His first words in the film—”Shut up!”—set the tone for a muddled relationship: Rocky, the prodigal son who’s disappointed the old man a few too many times, and Mickey, the absent father with whom it may be too late to make amends.

![Image 6: Rocky in his apartment ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-apartment-calling-small.jpg)

Rocky and “The Minstrels.”

**A.R.** It’s interesting how much _Rocky_ gets misremembered, largely because of [the numerous sequels](https://www.thefightcity.com/creed-ii-movie-boxing/), which are completely different films in terms of tone and depth. As a result, it seems we only remember the clichés, the caricatures. What strikes me when I re-watch _Rocky_ is that he isn’t “called” by Apollo until about halfway through. A full fifty-percent of the movie is just scene setting and character building. It’s a very 1970s pace for filmmaking, comparable to others of the same year like _Taxi Driver_ and _Marathon Man_. And when Rocky is finally “called,” remember, it isn’t because of his worthiness. Creed picks his name out of a book because he likes the rhyme of “Italian Stallion.” Rocky is a self-described “ham and egger.” He isn’t deserving and he knows it and he initially turns down the offer. We never see him agree to the fight on camera and a jump cut to the press conference confirms it’s happening. Likewise, we never hear the conversation where Rocky and Mickey agree to work together. They shout and argue and plead, but when they finally put aside the anger and bitterness in the dark of a nighttime Philadelphia street, the microphone goes silent.

**D.C.** Since you bring them up, I have to note that in terms of opening credit sequences, _Rocky_ is almost identical in style to _Taxi Driver_ and _Marathon Man_. Now Rocky’s worthiness as a challenger, or lack thereof, is an important element in the film’s pathos, but you’re right in that his doubts lie less with his ability to take on the champ—after all, he believes he has the ability to be a good sparring partner for Creed—than with his dignity and merit, and it’s that desire to make himself matter, to prove that he’s not “just another bum,” that elevates the film. That and the fact that the movie works as a powerful love story. These elements cohere so well that it’s impossible to tune out halfway through just because the plot takes its abundant liberties with the realities of the sport. In fact, the fight seems almost incidental, a bonus, when weighed against the love story. I imagine that element brought in more female viewers and likely helped it to earn the accolades it received.

![Image 7: Rocky and Adrian ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Adrian-and-Rocky-pet-shop.jpg)

Adrian and Rocky in the pet store.

**A.R.** I agree and I think _Rocky_ gets a bum rap as being this very generic, commercial pandering type of film, but it really is a good example of what is sometimes called “American New Wave” filmmaking, a style that dominated in the seventies. That’s what gives it a similar feel to pictures like _Marathon Man_ and _Taxi Driver_. There was a lot of cinematic innovation going on, and _Rocky_ was no exception. It was one of the first pictures to feature the newly-invented Steadicam, for instance. A number of the iconic _Rocky_ shots would not have been possible without that technology. Rocky running up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, for example, would have looked completely different without it. Now we’ve mentioned Mickey, Adrian, Paulie, and Apollo, and the movie couldn’t be what it is without that supporting cast. Do you have a favorite?

**D.C.** To me, Paulie is the most captivating. Like the others, his backstory is unknown, though that’s rectified in the sequels. He may seem like the least consequential of the five major characters, but without him, the story would be so tightly composed as to implode on itself. It’s interesting that Stallone originally wanted Harvey Keitel to take the role, though I think he would have been far too domineering: his mien, his physique, and his methodology are ill-suited to a loser like Paulie.

**A.R.** I think Burt Young was perfectly cast. He does this subtle gesture, puffing out his lower lip whenever he takes a nip from his bottle. It’s so perfectly infantile and pathetic. I would have given him the Academy Award for that alone.

![Image 8](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Paulie-beer.jpg)

Burt Young as Paulie.

**D.C.** Paulie plays like the Jungian shadow to both Rocky and his sister. His penchant for violence reverberates as much as Rocky’s attempt to escape it. This is most evident in his wish to work for Gazzo. As he says, “Breakin’ bones don’t bother me.” Anyone who saw 1974’s _The Gambler_ knows he’s well versed in that department. While his sister works in a pet shop nurturing innocent souls waiting to be rescued, sort of like the rest of the characters, Paulie spends his days swinging dead cow carcasses. The sibling relationship keeps him in a perpetual state of arrested development in which he figures so long as he’s taking care of his sister, he doesn’t have to move on with his own life. That’s why it causes him such distress when Adrian comes to develop her own volition. As siblings, they’re such opposites that Adrian’s mousiness is buried under Paulie’s wrath and domination. But she’s just as intriguing.

**A.R.** It’s interesting to consider Adrian in the context of past boxing movies as nearly all of them treat women as plot devices rather than full characters. A trope in boxing movies was giving the protagonist two love interests, the nice girl-next-door who knew him before he was famous, and then later, a gold-digging femme fatale. He then had to choose: be true to his core values or sell out to a life of fame and riches. _Rocky_ takes a different path, with Stallone’s character staying true to one woman.The movie, and the series as a whole, gets some flak for leaving Adrian undeveloped, but I think that looking at her in context reveals some layers that are easy to overlook.

![Image 9: Adrian and Rocky ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Adrian-and-Rocky-go-skating.jpeg)

Adrian and Rocky on their first date.

She begins the movie coupled to her brother Paulie, who feels chronically disrespected and needs Adrian’s near-total dependency to satisfy his own ego, to feel like he matters. Maybe he’s compensating for some lack of control in his life, but if Adrian is underwritten, it is here: the hows and whys that go unanswered in regards to tolerating her brother’s behavior for so long. If she yearns for something more, we come to understand it only through Rocky. But Paulie interprets Adrian’s independence as a threat and he lashes out at the couple that he helped to create. Adrian’s dramatic break with her brother —”What do I owe you?!”— is a powerful moment from a quiet character and I think one can see Adrian’s defiance of Paulie in 1976 as a meaningful feminist act.

**D.C.** Which only makes the movie’s love story that much more powerful, doesn’t it. It’s not just about two people falling in love, but about how that love transforms them, gives them new life. With Rocky’s help, Adrian breaks out of her shell and asserts herself, while it’s her love that gives Rocky the strength to suffer everything he must go through to give Apollo Creed the fight of his life, to “go the distance.” As I say, it’s the love story that makes the movie something more than the sum of its parts.

![Image 10: Rocky and Paulie ](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-and-Paulie.jpg)

Rocky and Paulie at the meat packing plant.

**A.R.** Yeah, the suffering of Rocky. That’s an important theme, isn’t it? And it brings us back to Christ and the Biblical allusions. Rocky is called but then, like so many saints and followers of Christ, he has to withstand what amounts to torture. The exaggerated violence and bloodiness of the fight scene, with Rocky enduring almost obscene punishment, his face a mass of welts before he begs Mickey to cut him with a razor, it’s all meant to function as something more than just gratuitous carnage.

**D.C.** And of course the pathos of that reflects how the movie has worked so hard to make Rocky such an endearing character, a sort of gentle giant with a heart of gold. Early in the film he encounters a barely conscious drunk lying on the pavement. He doesn’t step over him or walk past, but heaves the poor guy over his shoulder and carries him into the bar. Later he counsels a young girl, Marie, and even walks her home. She rejects his advice and calls him a “creepo,” but we see Rocky’s heart is always in the right place, that he cares. And so the viewer cares about him when he’s getting beaten to a pulp and pounded all over the ring.

**A.R.** Yeah, an intriguing, if minor, development in the sequels is when Stallone resurrects the character of Marie in _Rocky Balboa_, and Rocky works that goofy, bad joke charm thing again, like with Adrian in the pet store. Reportedly, there was serious consideration given to a Marie and Rocky romance for that film before Stallone and company, thankfully, rejected the idea.

**D.C.** Shifting gears, let’s talk about Rocky’s apartment. It’s the only hint the viewer has into his past which, for a film that remains completely rooted in the present, is virtually nil. We can tell he’s Catholic as evinced by the crucifixes on his walls, but I know you have other observations worth parsing out.

![Image 11](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/rocky-balboa-american-photos-mirror.jpg)

“… Christ does not look to our past but to the future.”

**A.R.** I love the set dressing that went into the apartment. It’s where much of the movie takes place and it’s a set we won’t see again in the Rocky series. A bachelor pad in extremus, it’s heaped with detritus, nearly decomposing. The walls are dirty, damaged. It’s a reflection of how Rocky is living at the time, of how his bad habits have become ingrained behaviors, or what Mickey calls “a waste of life.” Rocky stuffs beer bottles between the couch cushions. There’s no screen on the screen door. When he pulls ice out of his freezer, he drops a few ice cubes and doesn’t bother to pick them up. When Mickey drops in, Rocky throws darts into his bathroom door. Thankfully, we’re spared the sight of his bathroom. As you mentioned, there’s an obvious hint at the past in a set of photos tucked into the side of a mirror, real photos from Stallone’s childhood. Next to the mirror, knives are stabbed into the wall, U.S. military trench knives, in fact, an M1917 and a Mark I. Rocky hangs that famous black fedora on the Mark I. There’s a mattress tied around a pole, apparently a makeshift punching bag, with a giant buck knife sticking out of it. And when Rocky enters his apartment with Adrian for the first time, he hangs his coat on the handle of a machete stabbed into the wall. The knives speak to the violence that permeates Rocky’s world, but they also reveal his character. He isn’t wielding these knives as weapons but using them as hat racks. It suggests that while Rocky is in that world of violence and depravity, he isn’t _of_ that world, to paraphrase St. Paul.

**D.C.** Another prominent detail in the apartment, the portrait of [Rocky Marciano](https://www.thefightcity.com/rocky-marciano-floyd-boxing/), which brings us to Rocky’s name. According to Stallone, “The Brockton Blockbuster” was the sole inspiration for the character, though it seems to me Marciano is one of several facets that comprise the iconic moniker. In fact, Rocky’s hard-scrabble beginnings are closer to [Rocky Graziano’s](https://www.thefightcity.com/july-16-1947-zale-vs-graziano-ii-boxing-legendary/), whose birth name of Barbella, Stallone’s mother’s maiden name, collates neatly with Rocky’s surname, Balboa.

![Image 12](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Apollo-and-Rocky-prefight.jpg)

Carl Weathers as champion Apollo Creed.

**A.R.** And Graziano got his own biopic, _Somebody Up There Likes Me_ (1956), which helped launch the young Paul Newman’s career, much as _Rocky_ launched Stallone’s.

**D.C.** As to Rocky’s fighting moniker, “The Italian Stallion,” it was also used by a 1970s and 80s heavyweight and actor Lee Canalito, though it’s unclear as to who borrowed from whom, since the actors had worked together the previous year. Finally, “Stallone,” Italian for “stallion,” completes the colossal mash-up. When a reporter asks the fictional fighter how he came up with the sobriquet, Rocky responds that he “made that up one night while [he] was eating dinner.” Not likely.

The most obvious avatar is, of course, Chuck Wepner. But Stallone has never acknowledged it. Here I should point out that perfunctory internet searches will pull up quotes and listicles to the contrary, but I’m sticking with Wepner’s story. Was it a coincidence that the Ali vs Wepner bout took place on October 30, 1974, just a week or so before Stallone claims to have penned his script? Wepner even filed a lawsuit for “promotion of the Rocky movies… without consent and without compensation,” grumbling later that the settlement didn’t bring in “a minute percentage” of the fifteen million he wanted. While we’re on the topic of money, it’s worth remembering that Stallone had to forgo payment for his script and his acting in order to get the producers, Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff (who went on to produce [_Raging Bull_](https://www.thefightcity.com/raging-bull-jake-lamotta-film-memoir-boxing/) four years later) to make the film. But he earned $2.5 million from his percentage of box office takes, so he made out just fine.

![Image 13](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/rocky_2_stallone-and-mickey.jpg)

Burgess Meredith as trainer Mickey Goldmill.

**A.R.** It’s interesting to think about the context of Rocky’s release. Not a lot of on-screen characters were talking about the sport of boxing the way Stallone was. From 1949’s _The Set-Up_, to 1962’s [_Requiem for a Heavyweight_](https://www.thefightcity.com/rihn-curcio-requiem-for-a-heavyweight-boxing-cinema/), all the way to 1972’s [_Fat City_](https://www.thefightcity.com/the-edge-of-fat-city/), big-screen boxing was portrayed as pretty bleak. But _Rocky_ was a movie about holding onto hope and finding meaning in the ring, and Stallone was rewarded for that take. He was nominated for two Academy Awards: Best Screenplay and Best Actor, a rare combination of which Stallone was only the third to achieve, after Orson Welles and Charlie Chaplin. Not bad company for a guy who calls himself an “intellectual caveman.”

In all, _Rocky_ was nominated for ten Oscars, including nominations for Stallone, Talia Shire, Burt Young, and Burgess Meredith. It won three, Best Picture, Best Director and Best Film Editing, in a fairly stacked year, going up against _Taxi Driver_, _All the President’s Men_, _Network_, _Marathon Man_, and others. And here’s an interesting fact: _Rocky_ was the first sports movie to win Best Picture, but _not_ the first boxing movie, if we count _On The Waterfront_ (1954) as a boxing picture, which I do. And a boxing movie would not win Best Picture again until 2004’s _Million Dollar Baby_.

**D.C.** I’m a bit puzzled by Stallone’s attribution to [Muhammad Ali](https://www.thefightcity.com/top-12-reasons-muhammad-ali-forever-the-greatest-cassius-clay-joe-frazier-george-foreman-boxing/) as the inspiration for Apollo Creed, who espouses American pride at every turn, even entering the ring dressed as Uncle Sam in a two-dimensional model of the Durham boat. Such patriotism is at odds with Ali’s real-life, anti-American stances, his commitment to the Nation of Islam, and the separatist ideals that he espoused to Alex Haley in their _Playboy_ interviews. All of which is to say that I see no correlation between the real and fictional fighters.

![Image 14](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-vs-Apollo.jpg)

Rocky goes the distance.

**A.R.** That’s interesting because Ali recognized himself in Creed, the boastful Black champion who loves holding court with the press. “Starring Apollo Creed as Muhammad Ali,” he told Roger Ebert when the two watched _Rocky II_ together. And Ali was quick to analyze the success of _Rocky_: “I have been so great in boxing they had to create an image like Rocky, a white image on the screen, to counteract my image in the ring.”

**D.C.** The legacy of Ali has shifted in the past forty years from controversial, oft-despised provocateur, to brave “conscientious objector” and Civil Rights champion. Do you think this has affected the film’s legacy?

**A.R.** There’s no denying _Rocky’s_ cultural legacy, unmatched by any other boxing picture. How ubiquitous is that theme music? Or the phrase “Yo, Adriaaannnn”? For me, re-watching _Rocky_ never fails to yield something new. Sometimes it’s how Stallone refashions the tropes common to pre-Rocky boxing movies: the rise to the championship, the love interest, the influence of organized crime, even the training montage. Rather than avoid these shop-worn clichés, Rocky leans into their legacy, giving each a little twist, creating characters and storylines that feel at once both familiar and original. Other times, it’s noticing and appreciating the little things. How Rocky dresses his [Marciano](https://www.thefightcity.com/sept-23-1952-marciano-vs-walcott-joe-louis-rocky-marciano-jersey-joe-walcott-heavyweight-boxing/) portrait as Santa Claus. Or how after the big fight, Paulie distracts security so Adrian can slip into the ring. Or the morning zoo radio program that plays over the otherwise silent “raw eggs for breakfast” scene.

![Image 15](https://www.thefightcity.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Rocky-1-poster-steps.jpg)

Holding onto hope: Stallone’s uplifting take was a box office smash.

But perhaps what makes _Rocky_ so perennially relatable is that it’s ultimately about the nobility of the struggle and not the achievement. I think its final genius is that Rocky fights his heart out, but fails to win. I have watched it a hundred times and still I forget this, my memory buoyed or blurred by the cartoonish sequels and that triumphant theme music. But Rocky loses by split decision. And he doesn’t care. After all the training, the heartache, the pressure, all building towards this great struggle, Rocky discovers his apogee is elsewhere. Apollo can have his shiny belt; Rocky has won something more. Like the saints and martyrs of old, Rocky gains the greater victory through suffering and blood, through answering the call and having the courage to fight against the odds._**—****Andrew Rihn & David Curcio**_

## Description

**The boxing champion whose fight against the Nazis in and out of the ring made him a global icon**
During the 1930s and 1940s, no African American athlete commanded the spotlight more than heavyweight boxer Joe Louis. His 1938 knockout victory over German Max Schmeling struck an early blow against Nazi Germany. But it was Louis's service in the looming war that transformed him from a patriotic role model into history's first prominent Black athlete turned activist.

In _The Fight of His Life_, award-winning sports historians Johnny Smith and Randy Roberts tell the story of heavyweight champion Joe Louis's battles both in and out of the ring. Already world-famous at the outset of World War II, Louis enlisted in the army, serving as a goodwill ambassador and promoting unity across military bases that crackled with racial tension. Yet Louis's experience with segregation in the army sparked his political awakening. As the war dragged on, he advocated for Black soldiers facing discrimination. Once the war ended, he joined veterans and civil rights activists to fight for voting rights and racial equality.

Expertly revising the life story of one of America's most iconic Black athletes, Smith and Roberts's biography celebrates Joe Louis's forgotten fight against fascism abroad and racism at home.

## Description

**The boxing champion whose fight against the Nazis in and out of the ring made him a global icon**
During the 1930s and 1940s, no African American athlete commanded the spotlight more than heavyweight boxer Joe Louis. His 1938 knockout victory over German Max Schmeling struck an early blow against Nazi Germany. But it was Louis's service in the looming war that transformed him from a patriotic role model into history's first prominent Black athlete turned activist.

In _The Fight of His Life_, award-winning sports historians Johnny Smith and Randy Roberts tell the story of heavyweight champion Joe Louis's battles both in and out of the ring. Already world-famous at the outset of World War II, Louis enlisted in the army, serving as a goodwill ambassador and promoting unity across military bases that crackled with racial tension. Yet Louis's experience with segregation in the army sparked his political awakening. As the war dragged on, he advocated for Black soldiers facing discrimination. Once the war ended, he joined veterans and civil rights activists to fight for voting rights and racial equality.

Expertly revising the life story of one of America's most iconic Black athletes, Smith and Roberts's biography celebrates Joe Louis's forgotten fight against fascism abroad and racism at home.

# Out of the Shadows: 

# US Intelligence Sharing 

# and the Russia-Ukraine War, 2021–24 The Strategic Research and Assessment Department (SRAD) answers 

strategic questions, informs strategic decisions, and expands expert knowledge 

supporting US Army and Joint Force requirements. The organization is divided 

into a  Futures Research Group (FRG) that covers strategic competition, 

operational environmental security, emerging technologies, and AI integration 

and a Global Research Group (GRG) that includes the China Landpower 

Studies Center and researchers who study Europe, Eurasia, the Middle East, 

and the Western Hemisphere. 

SRAD contributes to the war-fighting capability by identifying 

strategic challenges and opportunities, clarifying the associated risk, 

and reducing uncertainty regarding the best way to move forward. 

Through research, publications, conferences, and direct engagement 

with major commands and the think-tank community, SRAD translates 

military, global, and technological trends into actionable insights enabling 

effective responses. For operational units, this support improves readiness 

by informing doctrine, campaign planning, force design, and leader 

development. For strategic-level staffs, SRAD provides independent analysis 

that supports policy development, theater strategy, security cooperation, 

force posture decisions, and long-term modernization efforts. 

By connecting scholarship, operational experience, and policymaking, 

SRAD serves as a strategic reconnaissance capability for the US Army— 

identifying emerging challenges, testing assumptions, and generating 

knowledge that improves the Army’s ability to compete, deter, and, 

if necessary, win future conflicts. 

SRAD is composed of civilian research professors, uniformed military 

officers, and a professional support staff, all with extensive credentials and 

experience. Researchers routinely engage organizations such as CENTCOM, 

the Joint Staff, Army Headquarters, combatant commands, and allied 

partners, providing expertise that helps decisionmakers align resources, 

priorities, and military capabilities with national objectives. i

# Foreword 

The Russia-Ukraine War will likely be one of the defining events of the twenty-first 

century, providing lessons and warnings applicable to future situations. Whereas the 

United States and its NATO allies eschewed the deployment of military forces to support 

Ukraine (a non-NATO country) after the conflict began in February 2022, they did provide 

substantial material assistance and other aid to Kyiv. One of the most critical aspects of this 

support was the Joe Biden administration’s willingness to disclose Russian plans publicly 

before the initiation of hostilities—a disclosure that aimed to deter, or at least disrupt, 

the intended military campaign. Many practitioners and scholars considered this disclosure 

a revolution in intelligence sharing, especially because the United States also supplied highly 

sensitive intelligence to Ukraine. But the disclosure did not result from the immediate 

Russian threat, as the US-Ukrainian intelligence partnership had started nearly a decade 

earlier—a fact unknown before the fighting occurred. 

In this monograph, Frank Leith Jones draws on reliable sources to provide a coherent 

narrative of US intelligence disclosure and sharing from 2021 to 2024, connecting both 

activities to a larger strategic framework and scrutinizing their effects at the operational 

and tactical levels of warfare. In doing so, Jones presents a comprehensive overview 

of US intelligence sharing with Ukraine and links related developments and reports 

to theoretical frameworks (such as deterrence theory), the policy-intelligence relationship, 

the integration of technology, and the role of organizational culture in intelligence 

operations. The monograph is a major case study of the uses of intelligence sharing and the 

ways in which intelligence cooperation with Ukraine and NATO allies supported a number 

of vital US policy goals. Critically, the monograph also addresses how intelligence sharing 

demanded an approach that balanced what the Biden administration hoped to achieve and 

the risks it was willing to take, such as the risk of compromising its sources and methods. 

As the case study demonstrates, the intelligence tool of statecraft is not used 

in isolation from the economic, military, and diplomatic tools; rather, intelligence is employed 

in conjunction with these other tools. Therefore, this monograph furnishes a series 

of lessons learned for US national security organizations and leaders to internalize. 

Emphasizing innovation, challenging existing paradigms, and connecting intelligence 

to political will are all actions that provide important guidelines for future action, as well 

as alert policymakers to potential perils. 

C. Anthony Pfaff 

Director, Strategic Research 

and Assessment Department 

and the US Army War College Press v

# Executive Summary 

Officials in the US Intelligence Community have described its intelligence 

sharing prior to and during the Russia-Ukraine War as unprecedented in the 

breadth and speed of release. On March 17, 2022, in a testimony before the 

House Armed Services Committee’s Subcommittee on Intelligence and Special 

Operations, General Paul Nakasone, director of the National Security Agency, 

stated he had “never seen it better” in his 35-year career. Nakasone was referring 

to the sharing of intelligence to assemble a coalition, “shine a light on disinformation 

operations,” and provide a partner with accurate, timely, and actionable intelligence. 

Besides addressing why the United States shared intelligence in general, 

Nakasone’s remarks outlined the Intelligence Community’s responsiveness 

to President Joe Biden’s three preliminary policy objectives: help Ukraine defend 

itself, bolster and unify NATO, and prevent a conflict with Russia. 

Using accessible, verifiable Western-based sources, this monograph examines 

US intelligence sharing before and during the Russia-Ukraine War, covering the 

period from 2021 through the end of Biden’s term in office. The monograph consists 

of three parts. The first part provides the strategic context, starting with a definition 

of intelligence sharing and the relevant US laws, directives, and executive orders 

that authorize such sharing with other countries. The author then examines the 

US-Ukrainian intelligence partnership that developed soon after Russia’s annexation 

of Crimea in 2014 and continued through 2024. Essential to understanding this 

relationship is recognizing its consistency with the US goal of enhancing intelligence 

collection against a strategic competitor. The discussion then considers the 

US Intelligence Community’s support to policymakers during the 2021–22 Ukraine 

crisis, a critical period in which the Intelligence Community provided warning and 

strategic intelligence assessments that led to Biden’s decision to disclose intelligence 

to Ukrainian political leaders and allies in support of his policy goals. 

Biden’s decision to share sanitized intelligence with international audiences 

to prevent Russia from invading Ukraine was the next occasion on which intelligence 

sharing occurred. This part of the monograph concludes by describing how 

US intelligence that was shared with Ukrainian armed forces at the operational 

and tactical levels of warfare helped these forces defend their country and, eventually, 

mount a counteroffensive. 

The monograph’s second part analyzes four important elements that made 

US intelligence sharing particularly successful. The first element involved the value 

of warning intelligence to policymakers, underscoring a key point: Such intelligence 

is not helpful unless it can persuade the decisionmaker to act, as it did in this 

case. The second element was intelligence for strategic messaging. The Biden vi Jones 

administration released downgraded intelligence to reveal Russian intentions and 

capabilities to global audiences for the purposes of both public diplomacy and 

information warfare. The third element involved intelligence sharing to reassure 

NATO allies and, more importantly, the deployment of numerous US intelligence, 

surveillance, and reconnaissance platforms, as well as cyber defense teams, 

to NATO countries. The deployment of high-end capabilities highlighted US resolve, 

commitment, and risk tolerance, while also demonstrating trust in allies through 

sharing intelligence from these assets and engaging in cyber counterintelligence 

operations. The fourth element was the way in which intelligence sharing 

helped the Ukrainian armed forces generate and apply additional combat power. 

Army Doctrine Publication 3-0,  Operations , defines combat power as “the total 

means of destructive, constructive, and information capabilities that a military 

unit or formation can apply at a given time.” In this case, intelligence, one of the 

elements of combat power, was crucial to the effectiveness of Ukrainian combat 

forces—from operational planning to tactical execution. 

The monograph’s third part details the redlines and risks associated with 

intelligence sharing. Specifically, this analysis elaborates on the limitations 

intelligence sharing at the strategic level—achieved through the public disclosure 

of declassified information—has in deterring or dissuading an adversary from 

acting. Further, the analysis highlights the significant risks the sharing of such 

information poses to sources and methods, regardless of how rigorous the vetting 

process for informational release may be. Each declassified report that is disclosed 

or shared identifies a subject—an organization or an individual against which the 

United States is clandestinely collecting information through human or technical 

sources. This identification allows the adversary to improve its security, strengthen 

its defense, and limit its vulnerabilities, thereby hindering current and future 

US collection efforts. 

Once a war begins, intelligence sharing principally moves from the strategic 

to the operational and tactical levels. In the case of Ukraine, this transformation 

explains how US policy ends steered intelligence sharing from the initial objective 

of supporting Ukrainian defense to the more expansive aim of weakening Russia 

and preventing it from taking future actions against other European countries. 

In the view of President Biden, Vladimir Putin was not just attacking Ukraine 

in February 2022; he was assaulting the elemental principles of sovereignty 

and independence that safeguard peace and stability in the international order. 

Even though the Biden administration established redlines to prevent Russia 

from claiming the United States was a cobelligerent, redlines shift when adjustments 

to the tactical situation render the stakes high. This shift is especially likely 

to occur when the supported state begins a counteroffensive, as indeed was the 

case in Ukraine. The US intelligence apparatus and military became part of the vii Executive Summary 

Ukrainian kill chain. With this step, the risk of the United States being drawn 

into the conflict increased—both because the tenets of international law were being 

tested and because the United States could not always control how the Ukrainian 

armed forces used US-provided intelligence in combat. The possibility of such 

intelligence being used contrary to US policy goals or in violation of international 

law was always present. Yet, even when controls on the use of intelligence existed, 

the United States abetted horizontal and vertical escalation—an example of the 

administration’s changed risk tolerance. 

The monograph’s third section also examines the two major lessons from 

US intelligence sharing as they relate to future crises. The first lesson suggests 

the public disclosure of intelligence to international audiences will not become 

the new normal, though it will continue to have a role for two reasons. 

Firstly, as Israeli scholar Ofek Riemer has demonstrated, the public disclosure 

of intelligence is a performative act that strengthens public diplomacy and helps 

global power projection consistent with the demands of the information age and 

the present-day media environment. Secondly, such disclosure endures as a useful 

instrument: At the strategic level, it can shape adversaries’ behavior while managing 

security threats below the threshold of military confrontation. 

The second lesson emphasizes the criticality of the US Intelligence Community’s 

organizational adaptation—achieved through innovative practices—to the dynamic 

strategic environment. The Intelligence Community embraced several innovative 

capabilities after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea, an event that proved 

to be a learning experience that was later institutionalized. Thus, however reluctant 

the intelligence bureaucracy may have been to carry out the decisionmaker’s 

demands—especially with respect to public disclosure—or however much the 

enhancement of Ukraine’s military capabilities required new organizational 

approaches, the Intelligence Community demonstrated a willingness to respond 

by modifying its traditional ways of doing business. 1

# PART 1 

# Defining US Intelligence Sharing 

# in the Russia-Ukraine War 

The United States’ involvement in intelligence sharing, which is also known 

as US foreign intelligence relations, formally began in World War I when 

the United States shared intelligence with France and the United Kingdom. 

Since then, intelligence sharing—that is, “cooperation between a U.S. and a foreign 

state or non-state intelligence service” regarding an issue of “mutual interest”— 

has become an increasingly essential element of US foreign policy, national security, 

and even the enhancement of US defense capabilities. 1 American intelligence sharing 

with Ukraine in the Russia-Ukraine War illustrates the essential role of this form 

of cooperation. 2

The United States grounds its intelligence-sharing decisions principally on the 

benefit that will accrue to the United States by entering an intelligence-sharing 

arrangement. Other important factors are US legal authorities, policies, historical 

relationships, and mutual security interests. 3 Nevertheless, like all partnerships, 

intelligence-sharing relationships involve tensions and potential obstacles 

to cooperation, such as differences in values, ethics, legal authorities, and policies. 

More critically, substantial risks are involved in intelligence sharing because 

intelligence could be compromised through espionage or a partner’s inadequate 

security measures. Yet, after several decades of experience with intelligence sharing, 

the US Intelligence Community (IC) often deems the benefit of cooperating 

with foreign partners as far outweighing the risk. 4

The primary means of sharing intelligence with allies and partners is through the 

“exchange of information, raw data, or finished intelligence,” but the arrangements

Most intelligence-sharing relationships are bilateral, but the Intelligence Community 

establishes multilateral relationships with allied organizations and even coalition 

partners when combat operations or other US interests necessitate these associations. 

As the Ukrainian case indicates, the occurrence of war and the need to prepare 

for conflict—especially among indications and warnings of an attack— 

continue to be the greatest motivations for intelligence sharing. 

In addition, a set of IC regulations, US laws, and other directives had 

an important bearing on the United States’ decision to disclose downgraded 

intelligence to the US and global publics, as well as to share finished intelligence 

with US allies and partners (in this case including Ukraine, which is not a US ally). 

By law, the director of national intelligence (DNI) is responsible for “oversee[ing] the 

coordination of the relationships between elements of the intelligence community 

and the intelligence or security services of foreign governments or international 

organizations on all matters involving intelligence related to the national security 

or involving intelligence.” 7 But the case of intelligence sharing with Ukraine 

is different in two respects. In this instance, most senior US intelligence officials and 

military officers believed the president must make the decision to share intelligence, 

given IC assessments indicated a war between Russia and Ukraine may occur. 8

Thus, the Intelligence Community’s first obligation was to provide an explicit and 

persuasive intelligence warning to President Joe Biden, communicating US national 

security objectives were under grave threat. 9 For this reason, Biden became the chief 

official in charge of deciding whether to release declassified US intelligence to the 

public. Second, Biden determined the extent to which the United States would 

share intelligence with Ukraine and others, to achieve the US policy objective 

of deterring Russia from invading Ukraine. 

To accomplish the United States’ main policy aim, the Biden administration 

initially used intelligence disclosure for three purposes. First, the public disclosure 

of intelligence served as a strategic messaging tool, countering disinformation that

Second, by sharing intelligence with allies and partners, the United States sought to build unity (principally among NATO member states), ensuring allies and partners would assist Ukraine militarily, economically, and diplomatically if the country was invaded. Third, in this context, intelligence sharing reassured NATO allies—especially states on NATO’s eastern flank—the Biden administration was aware of Russia’s potential actions against them, and the United States was committed to their defense under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. Biden and his senior advisers recognized the risks inherent in the public disclosure and sharing of intelligence but believed the benefits outweighed those risks, and the intelligence and military organizations involved adapted their processes to mitigate them. After Russia invaded Ukraine, the United States adopted a new policy objective: helping Ukraine defend itself against the Russian onslaught. The United States, among other countries (most importantly the United Kingdom and Estonia), shared intelligence with the Ukrainian government and military; intelligence sharing became a tactical enabler of Ukrainian combat operations. But the Biden administration incorporated policy constraints into its intelligence-sharing processes so Russia could not claim the United States was a cobelligerent. Yet, at the operational and tactical levels of warfare, US military and intelligence agencies became deeply enmeshed in Ukrainian military operations. As the situation on the ground developed, US policy objectives changed again. Informed by US intelligence, Ukraine mounted a counteroffensive against Russian forces in mid-2022; eventually in 2023, the Biden administration modified its policy constraints. These modifications enabled the United States to provide more sophisticated weaponry that used US intelligence to target Russian military assets, thus allowing Ukraine to escalate the conflict horizontally (and, to an extent, vertically). When Biden left office in January 2025, the principal question was whether the Donald Trump administration would continue sharing intelligence, and if so, under what conditions. analysts vetted the material, but the general’s approach occurred at an opportune

# Warning: Employing an Advantage 

The intelligence scholar Jack Davis observed the “central mission of intelligence 

analysis is to warn US officials about dangers to national security interests and 

to alert them to perceived openings to advance US policy objectives.” 182  This mission 

intends to counteract and mitigate surprise through warning intelligence: a specific 

intelligence discipline in which the US Intelligence Community uses indicators and 

warning methodology to collect, analyze, and disseminate intelligence products. 

Through this process, the Intelligence Community notifies policymakers and 

other officials of a foreign power’s imminent capabilities, intentions, and activities 

that may affect US national interests unfavorably. The intelligence must be timely, 

explicitly communicated, and persuasive so policymakers act. 183  Many observers 

agree Russia’s invasion of Ukraine vindicated US warnings about the attack. 

Before the invasion, the warnings irritated Kyiv, which feared the information 

only heightened tensions with Russia. Ukraine had dismissed Russian troop

Additionally, some NATO allies remained skeptical of US intelligence. 184

The one area in which a warning was exceedingly difficult to issue was the timing

In December 2021, the Biden administration first warned about a potential invasion,

did not occur on the specified date, the administration provided a more ambiguous 

range of possible dates, then finally, it stopped specifying dates. 194  This chain 

of modifications led to concerns about “crying wolf ”—a process in which warnings 

are issued but the consequences do not materialize. 195  Consequently, the audience 

becomes desensitized and ultimately scorns subsequent warnings because it judges

inner circle ( siloviki ) when the public disclosures surfaced. Putin and other officials 

took counteractions, but the downgraded intelligence surely forced them to modify 

or abandon certain plans or activities. 196  This result suggests the US Intelligence 

Community was inside the Kremlin’s observation-orientation-decision-action loop: 

a warfare concept US Air Force Colonel John Boyd introduced in the 1970s. 

Boyd refined his concept of operating inside an adversary’s observation-

orientation-decision-action loop over the years and, as Brian Price has pointed 

out, in the late 1980s, Boyd underscored the fact such operations could result 

in disruptions such as “uncertainty, doubt, mistrust, confusion,” and other effects. 197 

American intelligence that warned of the Russian invasion, and the publicly disclosed, 

declassified versions of this intelligence, served the purposes highlighted by Boyd. 

As Price points out, the outcomes of operating within the loop do not have to sow

substantial material assistance and other aid to Kyiv. One of the most critical aspects of this 

support was the Joe Biden administration’s willingness to disclose Russian plans publicly 

before the initiation of hostilities—a disclosure that aimed to deter, or at least disrupt, 

the intended military campaign. Many practitioners and scholars considered this disclosure 

a revolution in intelligence sharing, especially because the United States also supplied highly 

sensitive intelligence to Ukraine. But the disclosure did not result from the immediate 

Russian threat, as the US-Ukrainian intelligence partnership had started nearly a decade 

earlier—a fact unknown before the fighting occurred. 

In this monograph, Frank Leith Jones draws on reliable sources to provide a coherent 

narrative of US intelligence disclosure and sharing from 2021 to 2024, connecting both 

activities to a larger strategic framework and scrutinizing their effects at the operational 

and tactical levels of warfare. In doing so, Jones presents a comprehensive overview 

of US intelligence sharing with Ukraine and links related developments and reports 

to theoretical frameworks (such as deterrence theory), the policy-intelligence relationship, 

the integration of technology, and the role of organizational culture in intelligence 

operations. The monograph is a major case study of the uses of intelligence sharing and the 

ways in which intelligence cooperation with Ukraine and NATO allies supported a number 

of vital US policy goals. Critically, the monograph also addresses how intelligence sharing 

demanded an approach that balanced what the Biden administration hoped to achieve and 

the risks it was willing to take, such as the risk of compromising its sources and methods. 

As the case study demonstrates, the intelligence tool of statecraft is not used 

in isolation from the economic, military, and diplomatic tools; rather, intelligence is employed 

in conjunction with these other tools. Therefore, this monograph furnishes a series 

of lessons learned for US national security organizations and leaders to internalize. 

Emphasizing innovation, challenging existing paradigms, and connecting intelligence 

to political will are all actions that provide important guidelines for future action, as well 

as alert policymakers to potential perils.
