# Executive Summary 

Officials in the US Intelligence Community have described its intelligence 

sharing prior to and during the Russia-Ukraine War as unprecedented in the 

breadth and speed of release. On March 17, 2022, in a testimony before the 

House Armed Services Committee’s Subcommittee on Intelligence and Special 

Operations, General Paul Nakasone, director of the National Security Agency, 

stated he had “never seen it better” in his 35-year career. Nakasone was referring 

to the sharing of intelligence to assemble a coalition, “shine a light on disinformation 

operations,” and provide a partner with accurate, timely, and actionable intelligence. 

Besides addressing why the United States shared intelligence in general, 

Nakasone’s remarks outlined the Intelligence Community’s responsiveness 

to President Joe Biden’s three preliminary policy objectives: help Ukraine defend 

itself, bolster and unify NATO, and prevent a conflict with Russia. 

Using accessible, verifiable Western-based sources, this monograph examines 

US intelligence sharing before and during the Russia-Ukraine War, covering the 

period from 2021 through the end of Biden’s term in office. The monograph consists 

of three parts. The first part provides the strategic context, starting with a definition 

of intelligence sharing and the relevant US laws, directives, and executive orders 

that authorize such sharing with other countries. The author then examines the 

US-Ukrainian intelligence partnership that developed soon after Russia’s annexation 

of Crimea in 2014 and continued through 2024. Essential to understanding this 

relationship is recognizing its consistency with the US goal of enhancing intelligence 

collection against a strategic competitor. The discussion then considers the 

US Intelligence Community’s support to policymakers during the 2021–22 Ukraine 

crisis, a critical period in which the Intelligence Community provided warning and 

strategic intelligence assessments that led to Biden’s decision to disclose intelligence 

to Ukrainian political leaders and allies in support of his policy goals. 

Biden’s decision to share sanitized intelligence with international audiences 

to prevent Russia from invading Ukraine was the next occasion on which intelligence 

sharing occurred. This part of the monograph concludes by describing how 

US intelligence that was shared with Ukrainian armed forces at the operational 

and tactical levels of warfare helped these forces defend their country and, eventually, 

mount a counteroffensive. 

The monograph’s second part analyzes four important elements that made 

US intelligence sharing particularly successful. The first element involved the value 

of warning intelligence to policymakers, underscoring a key point: Such intelligence 

is not helpful unless it can persuade the decisionmaker to act, as it did in this 

case. The second element was intelligence for strategic messaging. The Biden vi Jones 

administration released downgraded intelligence to reveal Russian intentions and 

capabilities to global audiences for the purposes of both public diplomacy and 

information warfare. The third element involved intelligence sharing to reassure 

NATO allies and, more importantly, the deployment of numerous US intelligence, 

surveillance, and reconnaissance platforms, as well as cyber defense teams, 

to NATO countries. The deployment of high-end capabilities highlighted US resolve, 

commitment, and risk tolerance, while also demonstrating trust in allies through 

sharing intelligence from these assets and engaging in cyber counterintelligence 

operations. The fourth element was the way in which intelligence sharing 

helped the Ukrainian armed forces generate and apply additional combat power. 

Army Doctrine Publication 3-0,  Operations , defines combat power as “the total 

means of destructive, constructive, and information capabilities that a military 

unit or formation can apply at a given time.” In this case, intelligence, one of the 

elements of combat power, was crucial to the effectiveness of Ukrainian combat 

forces—from operational planning to tactical execution. 

The monograph’s third part details the redlines and risks associated with 

intelligence sharing. Specifically, this analysis elaborates on the limitations 

intelligence sharing at the strategic level—achieved through the public disclosure 

of declassified information—has in deterring or dissuading an adversary from 

acting. Further, the analysis highlights the significant risks the sharing of such 

information poses to sources and methods, regardless of how rigorous the vetting 

process for informational release may be. Each declassified report that is disclosed 

or shared identifies a subject—an organization or an individual against which the 

United States is clandestinely collecting information through human or technical 

sources. This identification allows the adversary to improve its security, strengthen 

its defense, and limit its vulnerabilities, thereby hindering current and future 

US collection efforts. 

Once a war begins, intelligence sharing principally moves from the strategic 

to the operational and tactical levels. In the case of Ukraine, this transformation 

explains how US policy ends steered intelligence sharing from the initial objective 

of supporting Ukrainian defense to the more expansive aim of weakening Russia 

and preventing it from taking future actions against other European countries. 

In the view of President Biden, Vladimir Putin was not just attacking Ukraine 

in February 2022; he was assaulting the elemental principles of sovereignty 

and independence that safeguard peace and stability in the international order. 

Even though the Biden administration established redlines to prevent Russia 

from claiming the United States was a cobelligerent, redlines shift when adjustments 

to the tactical situation render the stakes high. This shift is especially likely 

to occur when the supported state begins a counteroffensive, as indeed was the 

case in Ukraine. The US intelligence apparatus and military became part of the vii Executive Summary 

Ukrainian kill chain. With this step, the risk of the United States being drawn 

into the conflict increased—both because the tenets of international law were being 

tested and because the United States could not always control how the Ukrainian 

armed forces used US-provided intelligence in combat. The possibility of such 

intelligence being used contrary to US policy goals or in violation of international 

law was always present. Yet, even when controls on the use of intelligence existed, 

the United States abetted horizontal and vertical escalation—an example of the 

administration’s changed risk tolerance. 

The monograph’s third section also examines the two major lessons from 

US intelligence sharing as they relate to future crises. The first lesson suggests 

the public disclosure of intelligence to international audiences will not become 

the new normal, though it will continue to have a role for two reasons. 

Firstly, as Israeli scholar Ofek Riemer has demonstrated, the public disclosure 

of intelligence is a performative act that strengthens public diplomacy and helps 

global power projection consistent with the demands of the information age and 

the present-day media environment. Secondly, such disclosure endures as a useful 

instrument: At the strategic level, it can shape adversaries’ behavior while managing 

security threats below the threshold of military confrontation. 

The second lesson emphasizes the criticality of the US Intelligence Community’s 

organizational adaptation—achieved through innovative practices—to the dynamic 

strategic environment. The Intelligence Community embraced several innovative 

capabilities after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea, an event that proved 

to be a learning experience that was later institutionalized. Thus, however reluctant 

the intelligence bureaucracy may have been to carry out the decisionmaker’s 

demands—especially with respect to public disclosure—or however much the 

enhancement of Ukraine’s military capabilities required new organizational 

approaches, the Intelligence Community demonstrated a willingness to respond 

by modifying its traditional ways of doing business. 1

# PART 1 

# Defining US Intelligence Sharing 

# in the Russia-Ukraine War 

The United States’ involvement in intelligence sharing, which is also known 

as US foreign intelligence relations, formally began in World War I when 

the United States shared intelligence with France and the United Kingdom. 

Since then, intelligence sharing—that is, “cooperation between a U.S. and a foreign 

state or non-state intelligence service” regarding an issue of “mutual interest”— 

has become an increasingly essential element of US foreign policy, national security, 

and even the enhancement of US defense capabilities. 1 American intelligence sharing 

with Ukraine in the Russia-Ukraine War illustrates the essential role of this form 

of cooperation. 2

The United States grounds its intelligence-sharing decisions principally on the 

benefit that will accrue to the United States by entering an intelligence-sharing 

arrangement. Other important factors are US legal authorities, policies, historical 

relationships, and mutual security interests. 3 Nevertheless, like all partnerships, 

intelligence-sharing relationships involve tensions and potential obstacles 

to cooperation, such as differences in values, ethics, legal authorities, and policies. 

More critically, substantial risks are involved in intelligence sharing because 

intelligence could be compromised through espionage or a partner’s inadequate 

security measures. Yet, after several decades of experience with intelligence sharing, 

the US Intelligence Community (IC) often deems the benefit of cooperating 

with foreign partners as far outweighing the risk. 4

The primary means of sharing intelligence with allies and partners is through the 

“exchange of information, raw data, or finished intelligence,” but the arrangements

In addition, a set of IC regulations, US laws, and other directives had

organizations on all matters involving intelligence related to the national security 

or involving intelligence.” 7 But the case of intelligence sharing with Ukraine 

is different in two respects. In this instance, most senior US intelligence officials and 

military officers believed the president must make the decision to share intelligence, 

given IC assessments indicated a war between Russia and Ukraine may occur. 8

Thus, the Intelligence Community’s first obligation was to provide an explicit and 

persuasive intelligence warning to President Joe Biden, communicating US national 

security objectives were under grave threat. 9 For this reason, Biden became the chief 

official in charge of deciding whether to release declassified US intelligence to the 

public. Second, Biden determined the extent to which the United States would 

share intelligence with Ukraine and others, to achieve the US policy objective 

of deterring Russia from invading Ukraine.

Informed by US intelligence, Ukraine mounted a counteroffensive against Russian forces in mid-2022; eventually in 2023, the Biden administration modified its policy constraints. These modifications enabled the United States to provide more sophisticated weaponry that used US intelligence to target Russian military assets, thus allowing Ukraine to escalate the conflict horizontally (and, to an extent, vertically). Prelude to Invasion 

The United States first became concerned about a possible invasion of Ukraine 

in April 2021, when the Intelligence Community observed an upsurge in the number 

of Russian forces near the Ukrainian border. Director of National Intelligence 

(DNI) Avril Haines later stated the increase was not for “diplomatic effect.” 29 

She believed Putin was “clearly considering military action on some level,” 

possibly a limited incursion given the magnitude of the forces present. 30 

William J. Burns, director of the CIA, agreed with Haines and indicated publicly 

the administration was concerned about the troop buildup, leading to a consultation 

with NATO allies. In addition, the sizable force presence created concerns in the 

White House, prompting the United States and Russia to hold a June 2021 summit 

in Geneva. According to Jake Sullivan, the president’s national security adviser, 

one of the motives behind the conference was to “create an alternative path that 

would involve Russia deescalating around Ukraine” and stabilize the US-Russian 

relationship and the overall situation in Ukraine. 31  Healthy discussion about Ukraine 

occurred at the meeting and the White House believed the crisis had been defused, 

but the elation was temporary. 32  In July, Putin published a lengthy manifesto, 

“On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians,” which asserted Ukraine, 

along with Belarus, was part of a “triune Russian nation” based on history, 

language, ethnic identity, culture, and Eastern Orthodoxy. 33  In a social-media post, 

noted US journalist and historian Anne Applebaum characterized Putin’s essay 

as “essentially a call to arms” that provided the rationale for a Russian invasion 

of Ukraine. 34  Applebaum was not alone. The change in rhetoric could not be ignored, 

and US officials believed it signified a change “in [Putin’s] mindset.” 35

# Warning: Employing an Advantage 

The intelligence scholar Jack Davis observed the “central mission of intelligence 

analysis is to warn US officials about dangers to national security interests and 

to alert them to perceived openings to advance US policy objectives.” 182  This mission 

intends to counteract and mitigate surprise through warning intelligence: a specific 

intelligence discipline in which the US Intelligence Community uses indicators and 

warning methodology to collect, analyze, and disseminate intelligence products. 

Through this process, the Intelligence Community notifies policymakers and 

other officials of a foreign power’s imminent capabilities, intentions, and activities 

that may affect US national interests unfavorably. The intelligence must be timely, 

explicitly communicated, and persuasive so policymakers act. 183  Many observers 

agree Russia’s invasion of Ukraine vindicated US warnings about the attack. 

Before the invasion, the warnings irritated Kyiv, which feared the information 

only heightened tensions with Russia. Ukraine had dismissed Russian troop 

movements near its borders as routine events since the 2014 annexation of Crimea. 

Additionally, some NATO allies remained skeptical of US intelligence. 184

the Kremlin indicated it planned to withdraw its troops to their permanent bases. 186

**Joseph Robinette Biden Jr.**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-2) (born November 20, 1942) is an American retired politician who served as the 46th [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") from 2021 to 2025. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), he [represented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senate_career_of_Joe_Biden "US Senate career of Joe Biden")[Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") in the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from 1973 to 2009 and also served as the 47th [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") under President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") from 2009 to 2017.

Born in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"), Biden graduated from the [University of Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware "University of Delaware") in 1965 and the [Syracuse University College of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_University_College_of_Law "Syracuse University College of Law") in 1968. He was elected to the [New Castle County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_County_Council "New Castle County Council") in 1970 and the [U.S. Senate in 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1972 United States Senate election in Delaware"). [As a senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senate_career_of_Joe_Biden "US Senate career of Joe Biden"), Biden chaired the Senate [Judiciary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary "United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary") and [Foreign Relations Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Foreign_Relations "United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations"). He drafted and led passage of the [Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violent_Crime_Control_and_Law_Enforcement_Act "Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act") and the [Violence Against Women Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violence_Against_Women_Act "Violence Against Women Act"). Biden oversaw six [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") confirmation hearings, including contentious [hearings for Robert Bork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination "Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination") and [Clarence Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination"). He opposed the [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War") in 1991 but voted in favor of the [Iraq War Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War_Resolution "Iraq War Resolution") in 2002. Biden ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic presidential nomination in the [1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "1988 Democratic Party presidential primaries") and [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2008 Democratic Party presidential primaries") primaries. In 2008, Obama chose him as his running mate, and he served as a close advisor to Obama [while in office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_presidency_of_Joe_Biden "Vice presidency of Joe Biden"). In the [2020 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), Biden chose [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") as his running mate, and they defeated [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbents [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence").

As president, Biden signed the [American Rescue Plan Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021") in response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States") and [recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_recession "COVID-19 recession"). He signed bipartisan bills on [infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act") and [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHIPS_and_Science_Act "CHIPS and Science Act"). Biden proposed the [Build Back Better Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_Back_Better_Act "Build Back Better Act"), part of which was incorporated into the [Inflation Reduction Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_Reduction_Act "Inflation Reduction Act") passed in 2022. He [appointed Ketanji Brown Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketanji_Brown_Jackson_Supreme_Court_nomination "Ketanji Brown Jackson Supreme Court nomination") to the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"). In [his foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Joe_Biden_administration "Foreign policy of the Joe Biden administration"), the U.S. reentered the [Paris Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement") and enacted the [New Atlantic Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Atlantic_Charter "New Atlantic Charter"). Biden [withdrew U.S. troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%932021_U.S._troop_withdrawal_from_Afghanistan "2020–2021 U.S. troop withdrawal from Afghanistan") from [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021) "War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)") in a chaotic exit, after which the [Taliban swiftly retook control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Taliban_offensive "2021 Taliban offensive"). He [responded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "United States and the Russian invasion of Ukraine") to the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022%E2%80%93present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)") by imposing [sanctions on Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_during_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "International sanctions during the Russian invasion of Ukraine") and authorizing [Ukrainian aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_aid_to_Ukraine_during_the_Russo-Ukrainian_War "United States military aid to Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War"). In 2022, Biden supported [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland")'s and [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden")'s bids to join [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") and formally approved their membership. During the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"), he condemned the actions of [Hamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas"), [gave Israel strong military and diplomatic support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war "United States support for Israel in the Gaza war"), sent humanitarian aid to the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip"), and backed [a temporary ceasefire proposal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_2025_Gaza_war_ceasefire "January 2025 Gaza war ceasefire") before his presidency ended.

[Concerns about Biden's age and health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_and_health_concerns_about_Joe_Biden "Age and health concerns about Joe Biden") persisted throughout his presidency. He is the first president to turn 80 years old while in office. Biden initially [ran for reelection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2024_presidential_campaign "Joe Biden 2024 presidential campaign") in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election"), winning the [Democratic primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2024 Democratic Party presidential primaries") and becoming the party's presumptive nominee. After his performance in the [first presidential debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Joe_Biden%E2%80%93Donald_Trump_presidential_debate "2024 Joe Biden–Donald Trump presidential debate"), intensifying scrutiny from both political parties about his age and health led him to [withdraw his candidacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election "Withdrawal of Joe Biden from the 2024 United States presidential election"). Biden entered office with majority support, but his approval ratings declined significantly during his presidency, particularly over concerns about [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation_surge "2021–2023 inflation surge") and [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration_to_the_United_States "Illegal immigration to the United States"). He is the [oldest living former U.S. president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age#Age_of_presidents "List of presidents of the United States by age") since the [second inauguration of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump "Second inauguration of Donald Trump") in 2025, the [oldest living former U.S. vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_vice_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of vice presidents of the United States by age") since [Dick Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Cheney "Dick Cheney") died in 2025, and the oldest person to have served as president.

Joseph Robinette Biden Jr. was born on November 20, 1942,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cong-bio-3) at St. Mary's Hospital in [Scranton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scranton,_Pennsylvania "Scranton, Pennsylvania"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover20105-4) to Catherine Eugenia "Jean" Biden ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Finnegan)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-5) and Joseph Robinette Biden Sr.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-6) He is the oldest child in a [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") family of predominantly [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Americans "Irish Americans") descent. Biden has a sister, [Valerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerie_Biden_Owens "Valerie Biden Owens"), and two brothers, [James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Biden "James Biden") and Francis.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover20108%E2%80%939-7)

Joseph Sr. had been wealthy, and the family purchased a home in the affluent Long Island suburb of [Garden City, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_City,_New_York "Garden City, New York"), in 1946.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-8) After he suffered business setbacks around the time Biden was seven years old,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-promises2008-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover20107%E2%80%938-11) the family lived with Jean's parents in Scranton for several years.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-father-12) Scranton fell into economic decline during the 1950s, and Joseph Sr. could not find steady work.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-Chogath_Kog'sante-13) Beginning in 1953, when Biden was ten,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-14) the family lived in an apartment in [Claymont, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claymont,_Delaware "Claymont, Delaware"), before moving to a house in nearby [Mayfield, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield,_Delaware "Mayfield, Delaware").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-17) Joseph Sr. later became a successful [used-car salesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Used-car_salesman "Used-car salesman"), maintaining the family in a middle-class lifestyle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-father-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-Chogath_Kog'sante-13)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) Growing up, Biden observed [alcoholism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholism "Alcoholism") in his family, deciding at a young age to be [teetotal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teetotalism "Teetotalism").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-father-12)

At [Archmere Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archmere_Academy "Archmere Academy") in Claymont,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201027,_32-19) Biden played baseball and was a standout [halfback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halfback_(American_football) "Halfback (American football)") and [wide receiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wide_receiver "Wide receiver") on the [high school football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_school_football "High school football") team.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-father-12)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-20) Though a poor student, he was [class president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_president "Class president") in his junior and senior years.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201040%E2%80%9341-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor199099-22) He graduated in 1961.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201040%E2%80%9341-21) At the [University of Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Delaware "University of Delaware") in [Newark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_Delaware "Newark, Delaware"), Biden briefly played freshman football[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-24) and received a Bachelor of Arts degree with a [double major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_major "Double major") in history and [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science") in 1965.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-ap-timeline-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor199098-26) To overcome a childhood stutter, he memorized lines from [Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson "Ralph Waldo Emerson") and [William Butler Yeats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Butler_Yeats "William Butler Yeats").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-27)

## Law school and early career (1966–1973)

Main article: [Early career of Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_life_and_career_of_Joe_Biden "Early life and career of Joe Biden")

Biden earned a [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from [Syracuse University College of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_University_College_of_Law "Syracuse University College of Law") in 1968. In his first year of law school, he failed a course because he [plagiarized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagiarism "Plagiarism") a law review article, but the failing grade was later stricken. His grades were relatively poor, and he graduated 76th in a class of 85.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt091887-28) He was [admitted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admission_to_the_bar_in_the_United_States "Admission to the bar in the United States") to the [Delaware bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_bar "Delaware bar") in 1969.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cong-bio-3)

Biden clerked at a law firm headed by prominent local [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") William Prickett in 1968 and self-identified as a Republican.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-dmn-87-29)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-30) He disliked incumbent [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") Delaware governor [Charles L. Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_L._Terry "Charles L. Terry")'s conservative racial politics and supported a more liberal Republican, [Russell W. Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_W._Peterson "Russell W. Peterson"), who defeated Terry in 1968.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-dmn-87-29) Local Republicans attempted to recruit Biden, but he registered as an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician "Independent politician") because of his distaste for Republican presidential candidate [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-dmn-87-29)

### Law practices

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Joe_Biden_in_1968_Edition_of_Onondagan_Yearbook.jpg/250px-Joe_Biden_in_1968_Edition_of_Onondagan_Yearbook.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joe_Biden_in_1968_Edition_of_Onondagan_Yearbook.jpg)

Biden pictured by [Syracuse University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_University "Syracuse University") in 1968

In 1969, Biden resumed practicing law, first as a [public defender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_defender "Public defender") in [Wilmington, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_Delaware "Wilmington, Delaware"). Most of his clients were [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") from Wilmington's east side.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-32) Biden then joined a firm headed by Sid Balick, a locally active Democrat.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoritz198743-33)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-dmn-87-29) Balick named him to the Democratic Forum, a group trying to reform and revitalize the state party,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201086-34) and Biden switched his registration to Democratic.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-dmn-87-29) He also started his own firm, Biden and Walsh.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoritz198743-33)[Corporate law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_law "Corporate law"), however, did not appeal to him, and [criminal law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_law "Criminal law") did not pay well.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-father-12) He supplemented his income by managing properties.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-watn020109-35)

Biden ran for the fourth district seat on the [New Castle County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_County,_Delaware#County_Council "New Castle County, Delaware") in 1970 on a liberal platform that included support for public housing in the suburbs.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201059-36)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-37) Biden won the general election, defeating Republican Lawrence T. Messick, and took office on January 5, 1971.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-39) He served until January 1, 1973.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201052%E2%80%9364-41) During his time on the county council, Biden opposed large highway projects, which he argued might disrupt Wilmington neighborhoods.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201052%E2%80%9364-41)

Biden had not openly supported or opposed the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") until he ran for Senate and opposed [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon")'s conduct of the war.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover201050,_75-42) While studying at the University of Delaware and Syracuse University, Biden obtained five student [draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") deferments. Based on a physical examination, he was given a conditional medical deferment in 1968; in 2008, a spokesperson for Biden said his having had "[asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma") as a teenager" was the reason.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-43)

### 1972 U.S. Senate campaign in Delaware

Main article: [1972 United States Senate election in Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1972 United States Senate election in Delaware")

Biden defeated Republican incumbent [J. Caleb Boggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Caleb_Boggs "J. Caleb Boggs") to become the junior U.S. senator from Delaware in 1972. He was the only Democrat willing to challenge Boggs and, with minimal campaign funds, was thought to have no chance of winning.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cby-43-44)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-father-12) Family members managed and staffed the campaign, which relied on meeting voters face-to-face and hand-distributing position papers,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-npr-72-45) an approach made feasible by Delaware's small size.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-watn020109-35) He received help from the [AFL-CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL-CIO "AFL-CIO") and Democratic pollster [Patrick Caddell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Caddell "Patrick Caddell").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cby-43-44) His platform focused on the environment, withdrawal from Vietnam, civil rights, mass transit, equitable taxation, health care and public dissatisfaction with "politics as usual".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cby-43-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-npr-72-45) A few months before the election, Biden trailed Boggs by almost thirty percentage points,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cby-43-44) but his energy, young family, and ability to connect with voters' emotions worked to his advantage,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) and he won with 50.5% of the vote.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-npr-72-45)

### Teaching

From 1991 to 2008, as an [adjunct professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjunct_professor "Adjunct professor"), Biden co-taught a [seminar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminar "Seminar") on [constitutional law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_law "Constitutional law") at [Widener University School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widener_University_School_of_Law "Widener University School of Law").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-47)

## U.S. Senate (1973–2009)

Main article: [US Senate career of Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senate_career_of_Joe_Biden "US Senate career of Joe Biden")

Elected to the U.S. Senate in [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1972 United States Senate election in Delaware"), Biden was reelected in [1978](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1978 United States Senate election in Delaware"), [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1984 United States Senate election in Delaware"), [1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1990 United States Senate election in Delaware"), [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "1996 United States Senate election in Delaware"), [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2002 United States Senate election in Delaware"), and [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_Senate_election_in_Delaware "2008 United States Senate election in Delaware"), regularly receiving about 60% of the vote.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-366-48) Aged 30 when first elected, he was the [seventh-youngest senator in U.S. history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_youngest_members_of_the_United_States_Congress#List_of_youngest_U.S._senators "List of youngest members of the United States Congress").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-49) He was junior senator to [William Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roth "William Roth") until Roth was defeated in 2000.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-50) He remains one of the [longest-serving senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_members_of_the_United_States_Congress_by_longevity_of_service "List of members of the United States Congress by longevity of service") in U.S. history.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-51) For 36 years, he commuted from Washington to Wilmington via [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak"), earning him the nickname "Amtrak Joe".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-Amtrak-1)

### Senate activities

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Joe_Biden_Takes_the_Oath_of_Office_as_Senator_of_Delaware_%281973%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Joe_Biden_Takes_the_Oath_of_Office_as_Senator_of_Delaware_%281973%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joe_Biden_Takes_the_Oath_of_Office_as_Senator_of_Delaware_(1973)_(cropped).jpg)

Secretary of the Senate [Francis R. Valeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_R._Valeo "Francis R. Valeo") swearing in Biden into the Senate on January 5, 1973

During his early years in the Senate, Biden focused on consumer protection and environmental issues and called for greater government accountability.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-52) In 1974, he described himself as liberal on civil rights and liberties, senior citizens' concerns, and healthcare, but conservative on other issues, including abortion and [military conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_conscription "Military conscription").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-53) Biden was the first U.S. senator to endorse Governor [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") for president in the [1976 Democratic primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "1976 Democratic Party presidential primaries"). Carter won the Democratic nomination and the [1976 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_United_States_presidential_election "1976 United States presidential election").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-54) Biden also worked on [arms control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_control "Arms control").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-foreign-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-56) After Congress failed to ratify the [SALT II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SALT_II "SALT II") Treaty signed in 1979 by [Soviet general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_general_secretary "Soviet general secretary")[Leonid Brezhnev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Brezhnev "Leonid Brezhnev") and President Carter, Biden met with Soviet foreign minister [Andrei Gromyko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Gromyko "Andrei Gromyko") and secured changes that addressed the Senate Foreign Relations Committee's objections.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-57) He received considerable attention when he excoriated Secretary of State [George Shultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Shultz "George Shultz") at a Senate hearing for the Reagan administration's support of [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") despite its policy of [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-dmn-87-29) In a congressional hearing in 1984, he objected to the [Strategic Defense Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Defense_Initiative "Strategic Defense Initiative") plan to construct autonomous systems of ICBM defense.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-59) Biden was an advocate for Delaware military installations, including [Dover Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Air_Force_Base "Dover Air Force Base") and [New Castle Air National Guard Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Castle_Air_National_Guard_Base "New Castle Air National Guard Base").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-60)

In the mid-1970s, Biden was one of the Senate's strongest opponents of [race-integration busing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race-integration_busing "Race-integration busing"). His Delaware constituents strongly opposed it, and such opposition nationwide later led his party to mostly abandon school integration policies.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-Gadsden-61) In his first Senate campaign, Biden had expressed support for busing to remedy _de jure_ segregation, as in the South, but opposed its use to remedy _de facto_ segregation arising from racial patterns of neighborhood residency, as in Delaware; he opposed a proposed constitutional amendment banning busing entirely.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGadsden2012214-62) Biden supported a 1976 measure forbidding the use of federal funds for transporting students beyond the school closest to them.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-Gadsden-61) He co-sponsored a 1977 amendment closing loopholes in that measure, which President Carter signed into law in 1978.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-63)

Biden became [ranking minority member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking_minority_member "Ranking minority member") of the [Senate Judiciary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Judiciary_Committee "Senate Judiciary Committee") in 1981. He was a Democratic floor manager for the successful passage of the [Comprehensive Crime Control Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Crime_Control_Act "Comprehensive Crime Control Act") in 1984. His supporters praised him for modifying some of the law's worst provisions, and it was his most important legislative accomplishment to that time.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-cby-44-64) In 1994, Biden helped pass the [Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violent_Crime_Control_and_Law_Enforcement_Act "Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act"), which included [a ban on assault weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Assault_Weapons_Ban "Federal Assault Weapons Ban"),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-66) and the [Violence Against Women Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violence_Against_Women_Act "Violence Against Women Act"),[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-67) which he has called his most significant legislation.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-68) The 1994 crime law was unpopular among progressives and criticized for resulting in mass incarceration;[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-70) Biden later expressed regret for passing the bill.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-71)

Biden voted for a 1993 provision that deemed homosexuality incompatible with military life, thereby banning [gay people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_gay,_lesbian_or_bisexual_people "List of gay, lesbian or bisexual people") from serving in the armed forces.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-73) In 1996, he voted for the [Defense of Marriage Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_of_Marriage_Act "Defense of Marriage Act"), which prohibited the federal government from recognizing same-sex marriages, thereby barring people in such marriages from equal protection under federal law and allowing states to do the same.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-NYT_Biden_Evolution_on_LGBTQ-74) In 2015, the act was ruled unconstitutional in _[Obergefell v. Hodges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obergefell\_v.\_Hodges "Obergefell v. Hodges")_.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-75)

Biden was critical of [Independent Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_the_Independent_Counsel "United States Office of the Independent Counsel")[Ken Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Starr "Ken Starr") during the 1990s [Whitewater controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitewater_controversy "Whitewater controversy") and [Clinton–Lewinsky scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton%E2%80%93Lewinsky_scandal "Clinton–Lewinsky scandal") investigations, saying "it's going to be a cold day in hell" before another independent counsel would be granted similar powers.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-76) He voted to acquit during the [impeachment of Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment_of_Bill_Clinton "Impeachment of Bill Clinton").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-77) During the 2000s, Biden sponsored bankruptcy legislation sought by credit card issuers (such as [MBNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBNA "MBNA"), one of Delaware's largest companies).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-78)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18)[Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") vetoed the bill in 2000, but it passed in 2005 as the [Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_Abuse_Prevention_and_Consumer_Protection_Act "Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) with Biden being one of only 18 Democrats to vote for it, while leading Democrats and consumer rights organizations opposed it.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-79) As a senator, Biden strongly supported increased [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") funding and rail ### Brain surgeries

In February 1988, after several episodes of severe neck pain, Biden underwent surgery to correct a leaking [intracranial berry aneurysm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intracranial_berry_aneurysm "Intracranial berry aneurysm").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-81)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-4cmed-82) While recuperating, he suffered a [pulmonary embolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_embolism "Pulmonary embolism").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-4cmed-82) A second aneurysm was surgically repaired in May.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-4cmed-82)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-83) His recuperation kept him away from the Senate for seven months.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-84)

### Senate Judiciary Committee

[![Image 12: Photo of Biden shaking hands with Reagan in the Oval Office](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/President_Ronald_Reagan_meeting_with_Senators_Joseph_Biden_and_William_Cohen_to_discuss_arms_control_and_the_results_of_their_trip_to_the_Soviet_Union_last_month_in_oval_office_-_DPLA_-_3c0002ee171c06689feb0b9c9eca5961.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_meeting_with_Senators_Joseph_Biden_and_William_Cohen_to_discuss_arms_control_and_the_results_of_their_trip_to_the_Soviet_Union_last_month_in_oval_office_-_DPLA_-_3c0002ee171c06689feb0b9c9eca5961.jpg)

Biden shaking hands with President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") in 1984

Biden was a longtime member of the [Senate Committee on the Judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary "United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary"). He chaired it from 1987 to 1995 and was a [ranking minority member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking_member "Ranking member") from 1981 to 1987 and again from 1995 to 1997.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-85)

As chair, Biden presided over two highly contentious [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") confirmation hearings.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) When [Robert Bork was nominated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination "Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination") in 1988, Biden reversed his approval‍—‌given in an interview the previous year‍—‌of a hypothetical Bork nomination. Conservatives were angered,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBronner1989138%E2%80%93139,_214,_305-86) but at the hearings' close Biden was praised for his fairness, humor, and courage.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBronner1989138%E2%80%93139,_214,_305-86)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-lg-87-87) Rejecting the arguments of some Bork opponents,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) Biden framed his objections to Bork in terms of the conflict between Bork's strong [originalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Originalism "Originalism") and the view that the [U.S. Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States") provides rights to liberty and privacy beyond those explicitly enumerated in its text.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-lg-87-87) Bork's nomination was rejected in the committee by a 5–9 vote[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-lg-87-87) and then in the full Senate, 42–58.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-88)

During [Clarence Thomas's nomination hearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination") in 1991, Biden's questions on constitutional issues were often convoluted to the point that Thomas sometimes lost track of them,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMayerAbramson1994213,_218,_336-89) and Thomas later wrote that Biden's questions were akin to "[beanballs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beanball "Beanball")".[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-90) After the committee hearing closed, the public learned that [Anita Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Hill "Anita Hill") had accused Thomas of [making unwelcome sexual comments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_harassment "Sexual harassment") when they had worked together.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-91)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-92) Biden had known of some of these charges, but initially shared them only with the committee because Hill was then unwilling to testify.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) The committee hearing was reopened and Hill testified, but Biden did not permit testimony from other witnesses, such as a woman who had made similar charges and experts on harassment.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-hill-93) The full Senate confirmed Thomas by a 52–48 vote, with Biden opposed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-bio-18) Liberal legal advocates and women's groups felt strongly that Biden had mishandled the hearings and not done enough to support Hill.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-hill-93) In 2019, he told Hill he regretted his treatment of her, but Hill said afterward she remained unsatisfied.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-94)

### Senate Foreign Relations Committee

Biden was a longtime member of the [Senate Foreign Relations Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Foreign_Relations "United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations"). He became its ranking minority member in 1997, and chaired it from June 2001 to 2003 and 2007 to 2009.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-365-95) His positions were generally [liberal internationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_internationalism "Liberal internationalism").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-foreign-55)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96) He collaborated effectively with Republicans and sometimes went against elements of his own party.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-365-95)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96) During this time he met with at least 150 leaders from 60 countries and international organizations, becoming a well-known Democratic voice on foreign policy.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-97)

Biden voted against authorization for the [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War") in 1991.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96) He became interested in the [Yugoslav Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslav_Wars "Yugoslav Wars") after hearing about Serbian abuses during the [Croatian War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatian_War_of_Independence "Croatian War of Independence") in 1991.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-foreign-55) Once the [Bosnian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War") broke out, Biden was among the first to call for the "[lift and strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lift_and_strike_(Bosnian_War) "Lift and strike (Bosnian War)")" policy.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-foreign-55)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-365-95)[George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") and [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") were both reluctant to implement the policy, fearing Balkan entanglement.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-foreign-55)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96) In April 1993, Biden had a tense three-hour meeting with Serbian leader [Slobodan Milošević](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slobodan_Milo%C5%A1evi%C4%87 "Slobodan Milošević").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-wapo-bosnia-98) Biden worked on several versions of legislative language urging the U.S. toward greater involvement.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-wapo-bosnia-98) He has called his role in affecting Balkan policy in the mid-1990s his "proudest moment in public life" related to foreign policy.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96) In 1999, during the [Kosovo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_War "Kosovo War"), Biden supported the [NATO bombing of Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_bombing_of_Yugoslavia "NATO bombing of Yugoslavia").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nyt-foreign-55) He and Senator [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") co-sponsored the McCain-Biden Kosovo Resolution, which called on Clinton to use all necessary force, including ground troops, to confront Milošević over Yugoslav actions toward [Kosovo Albanians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosovo_Albanians "Kosovo Albanians").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-wsj082508-99)

#### Wars in Afghanistan and Iraq

Main article: [War on terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror")

Biden was a strong supporter of the [War in Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021) "War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)"), saying, "Whatever it takes, we should do it."[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-100) As head of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, he said in 2002 that Iraqi president [Saddam Hussein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein "Saddam Hussein") was a threat to national security and there was no other option than to "eliminate" that threat.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-101) In October 2002, he voted in favor of the [Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authorization_for_Use_of_Military_Force_Against_Iraq "Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq"), approving the [U.S. invasion of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._invasion_of_Iraq "U.S. invasion of Iraq").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96) As chair of the committee, he assembled witnesses to testify in favor of the authorization. They gave testimony grossly misrepresenting the intent, history, and status of Saddam and his government, and touted Iraq's fictional possession of [weapons of mass destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapons_of_mass_destruction "Weapons of mass destruction").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-102) Biden eventually became a critic of the war, calling his vote a "mistake" by 2005,[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-103)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-104) but did not push for withdrawal.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-wapo-bosnia-98) He supported the appropriations for the occupation, but argued that the war should be internationalized, that more soldiers were needed, and that the Bush administration should "level with the [American people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans")" about its cost and length.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-aap08-365-95)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-wsj082508-99)

By late 2006, Biden's stance had shifted considerably. He opposed the [troop surge of 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troop_surge_of_2007 "Troop surge of 2007"),[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-lat-foreign-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-wapo-bosnia-98) saying General [David Petraeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Petraeus "David Petraeus") was "dead, flat wrong" in believing the surge could work.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nytm-traub-105) Biden, through a plan developed with [Council on Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Foreign_Relations "Council on Foreign Relations") president [Leslie H. Gelb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_H._Gelb "Leslie H. Gelb"), instead advocated dividing Iraq into a loose [federation of three ethnic states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalism_in_Iraq "Federalism in Iraq").[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-110) In September 2007, a non-binding resolution endorsing the plan passed the Senate,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-111) but the idea failed to gain traction.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-nytm-traub-105)

Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy "Robert F. Kennedy") (for which his aides took blame) and the [inaugural address of John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inaugural_address_of_John_F._Kennedy "Inaugural address of John F. Kennedy"). Biden made several false or exaggerated claims about his early life: that he had earned three degrees in college, that he attended [law school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_school "Law school") on a full scholarship, that he had graduated in the top half of his class,[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-122)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-123) and that he had marched in the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-124) The limited amount of other news about the presidential race amplified these disclosures,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-125) and on September 23, 1987, Biden withdrew his candidacy.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden#cite_note-126)
