[USS _Capodanno_(FF-1093)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Capodanno "USS Capodanno") was named in his honor. _Capodanno_ was commissioned November 17, 1973, and became the first ship in the US fleet to receive a Papal Blessing when it was blessed by [Pope John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II "Pope John Paul II") on September 4, 1981, the 14th anniversary of the chaplain's death. On July 30, 1993, the ship was decommissioned after 20 years of service and transferred to [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ship-3)

### New York City honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: New York City honors")]

In March 1971, the [Knights of Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_of_Columbus "Knights of Columbus"), Madonna Council in Staten Island began a public campaign for a permanent memorial honoring Capodanno in his home borough. In October 1974, a bill was proposed to change the name of Seaside Boulevard to [Father Capodanno Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Capodanno_Boulevard "Father Capodanno Boulevard"); a year later, the bill was passed by the Mayor of New York. For the [United States Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bicentennial "United States Bicentennial") weekend, the city of New York declared July 3, 1976, "Father Capodanno Day", and a memorial Mass was followed by a parade that included the United States Marine Corps Color Guard, marching bands, [Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America") and [Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl_Scouts_of_the_USA "Girl Scouts of the USA") Scouts, and many other groups.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-CatholicMil-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-23)

Near the midpoint of Staten Island's Father Capodanno Boulevard, at the corner of Sand Lane, a monument in the chaplain's honor is made of light gray Barre granite, stands 8' high and 4' wide (2.4m x 1.2m) and has a bronze plaque. Near the north end of the boulevard, alongside [Fort Wadsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Wadsworth "Fort Wadsworth")'s Father Capodanno Memorial Chapel, stands a 1977 statue of the chaplain praying for a fallen corpsman during their final battle.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ModeMemorials-24) The nearby [South Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Beach,_Staten_Island "South Beach, Staten Island") neighborhood is the location of Father Vincent Capodanno Catholic Academy, formed by the merger of two parish elementary schools in 2020.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-25)

### Saint Vincent Chapel, Taiwan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Saint Vincent Chapel, Taiwan")]

Saint Vincent Chapel, in Father Capodanno's Taiwanese mission territory, was his family's first choice as a memorial. Within four months after his death in 1967, almost $4,000 (equivalent to $40,000 in 2025) had been raised by organizations such as [The American Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_American_Legion "The American Legion"), The [Veterans of Foreign Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_of_Foreign_Wars "Veterans of Foreign Wars"), the Knights of Columbus, and the [Marine Corps League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Corps_League "Marine Corps League"). After various delays, the chapel was completed in 1993–1995. It was built in the small mountain town of Thiankou with the help of Father Daniel Dolan, another Maryknoller and Capodanno's former pastor in Taiwan.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-CatholicMil-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ModeMemorials-24)

### Capodanno Hall, San Francisco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Capodanno Hall, San Francisco")]

The San Francisco Bay Naval Shipyard ([Hunters Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunters_Point_Naval_Shipyard "Hunters Point Naval Shipyard"), 1941–1994) dedicated Capodanno Hall on November 3, 1969. The hall served as a Bachelor Officers' Quarters. Philip Capodanno unveiled the plaque that describes his brother's heroic deed:[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-CatholicMil-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ModeMemorials-24)

> Lieutenant Capodanno made the ultimate sacrifice ministering to the wounded and dying during savage fighting in Vietnam. He has become the third chaplain in our country's history to receive the Medal of Honor and the second Navy chaplain to be so honored.

**Vincent Robert Capodanno Jr.**, M.M. (February 13, 1929 – September 4, 1967) was an American [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") priest and [Maryknoll Missioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryknoll "Maryknoll") killed in action while serving as a [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") chaplain with a [Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") infantry unit during the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). He was a posthumous recipient of America's highest military decoration, the [Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor "Medal of Honor"), for heroic actions above and beyond the call of duty. As a [beatification process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatification "Beatification") has been opened for Capodanno, the Catholic Church has titled him a [Servant of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servant_of_God "Servant of God").

Vincent R. Capodanno Jr. was born in [Elm Park, Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elm_Park,_Staten_Island "Elm Park, Staten Island"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-1) on February 13, 1929, the tenth and youngest child of an immigrant father from [Gaeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaeta "Gaeta"), Italy, and an Italian-American mother. Capodanno graduated from [Curtis High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_High_School "Curtis High School") on February 4, 1947, then took night classes at [Fordham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordham_University "Fordham University") for a year while working as an insurance clerk. In 1949, he entered the [Maryknoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryknoll "Maryknoll") Missionary [Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminary "Seminary") in Ossining, New York, which included extensive studies in Illinois and Massachusetts. He was ordained a [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church")[priest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priesthood_(Catholic_Church) "Priesthood (Catholic Church)") by Cardinal [Francis Spellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Spellman "Francis Spellman") on June 14, 1958.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-milarch.org-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ship-3)

Capodanno's first assignment as a [missionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary "Missionary") was in 1959 with the [Hakka people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakka_people "Hakka people") in the mountains of [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), where he served in a parish and later in a school. After six years, he returned to the United States for leave and was assigned to a Maryknoll school in [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong"). Shortly after, he volunteered to serve as a military chaplain in [South Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Vietnam "South Vietnam") as the American presence escalated.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-milarch.org-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ship-3)

### Military service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Military service")]

On December 28, 1965, Capodanno received his commission as a lieutenant in the [Navy Chaplain Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Chaplain_Corps "United States Navy Chaplain Corps"). He then requested to serve with the [Fleet Marine Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleet_Marine_Force "Fleet Marine Force") (FMF) in South Vietnam. After some training to serve within the Marine Corps, he was assigned in April 1966 to the [1st Battalion, 7th Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Battalion,_7th_Marines "1st Battalion, 7th Marines"), [1st Marine Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Marine_Division_(United_States) "1st Marine Division (United States)") in South Vietnam. In December, he was transferred to the [1st Medical Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Medical_Battalion "1st Medical Battalion"), 1st Marine Division, until his year's tour was completed. In June 1967 after a one-month leave, he returned to Vietnam for a voluntary six-month extension, and in July was assigned to the [1st Battalion, 5th Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Battalion,_5th_Marines "1st Battalion, 5th Marines"). In August, he was assigned to [H&S Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headquarters_and_Service_Company "Headquarters and Service Company"), [3rd Battalion, 5th Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Battalion,_5th_Marines "3rd Battalion, 5th Marines"), 1st Marine Division, where he befriended Lieutenant [Frederick W. Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_W._Smith "Frederick W. Smith"), the future founder of [FedEx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx "FedEx"). Even before Capodanno's death, he was widely known for his willingness to share the hardships of suffering Marines on the front lines – "Radiating Christ" to those around him, in the terminology of Father Raoul Plus, a World War One chaplain studied by Maryknollers – or simply the "Grunt Padre", in the words of Capodanno's Marine companions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-milarch.org-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ship-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-5)

On [Labor Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Day "Labor Day"), September 4, 1967, at 04:30, during [Operation Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Swift "Operation Swift") in the [Thang Binh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thang_Binh "Thang Binh") District of the [Que Son Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Que_Son_Valley "Que Son Valley"), Company D, 1st Battalion, 5th Marines was attacked in its night defensive position by a large [People's Army of Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Army_of_Vietnam "People's Army of Vietnam") (PAVN) unit of approximately 2,500 near the village of [Dong Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dong_Son,_Quang_Nam?action=edit&redlink=1 "Dong Son, Quang Nam (page does not exist)"). The outnumbered and disorganized company needed support, and Company B was sent to assist. By 09:14, 26 Marines were confirmed dead. At 09:25, the commander of the 1st Battalion requested additional reinforcements, and Companies K and M from 3rd Battalion were committed to the battle, still leaving the Marines greatly outnumbered by the PAVN.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-6)

When Capodanno heard that two platoons of M Company from his battalion were taking casualties and about to be overrun by the PAVN, the unarmed chaplain went among the wounded and dying Marines of 2nd Platoon, helping and comforting them and giving [last rites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_rites "Last rites"). That afternoon, he was wounded in the hand, arms and legs. Refusing medical evacuation, in the early evening, he went to help a seriously wounded [Navy corpsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_corpsman "Hospital corpsman") and two wounded Marines only yards (meters) from an enemy machine gun and was killed;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-milarch.org-2) 14 Marines and two corpsmen from the battalion were also killed.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-vwall-7) His body was recovered and buried in his family's plot in [St. Peter's Cemetery (Staten Island)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Cemetery_(Staten_Island) "St. Peter's Cemetery (Staten Island)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-9)

On December 27, 1968, [Secretary of the Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Navy "Secretary of the Navy")[Paul Ignatius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ignatius "Paul Ignatius") notified the Capodanno family that he would posthumously be awarded the [Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor "Medal of Honor"). The ceremony was held on January 7, 1969.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-10)

## Canonization process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Canonization process")]

On May 19, 2002, Capodanno's [canonization process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization "Canonization") was opened. In May 2004, the initial documentation was submitted to the [Congregation for the Causes of Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_for_the_Causes_of_Saints "Congregation for the Causes of Saints"), with CatholicMil (later renamed Mission Capodanno) acting as Petitioner and with Capodanno's biographer Daniel Mode named [postulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postulator "Postulator"). On [Memorial Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Day "Memorial Day") weekend, May 21, 2006, Capodanno's designation as a [Servant of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servant_of_God "Servant of God") was announced in Washington D.C., by Archbishop [Edwin F. O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_F._O'Brien "Edwin F. O'Brien") of the [Archdiocese for the Military Services, USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdiocese_for_the_Military_Services,_USA "Archdiocese for the Military Services, USA"). On October 1, 2013, O'Brien's successor, Archbishop [Timothy P. Broglio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_P._Broglio "Timothy P. Broglio"), presided over the formal renewal of the opening of the cause for beatification. Broglio announced at this time that the newly established Capodanno Guild would serve as the Petitioner of the Cause and Andrea Ambrosi as Roman Postulator.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-12) Following a year-long investigation, Bishop [Gerald Barbarito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Barbarito "Gerald Barbarito") in 2019 officially credited Capodanno with the miraculous healing of a Florida woman with [multiple sclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_sclerosis "Multiple sclerosis").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-13)

In 2017, for the 50th anniversary of Capodanno's death, [EWTN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EWTN "EWTN") collaborated with the Capodanno Guild to produce _Called and Chosen_, a documentary film publicizing his life and the ongoing effort. The film won the [Catholic Press Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Press_Association "Catholic Press Association")'s 2018 [Gabriel Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Award "Gabriel Award") for Best Religious TV, National Release.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-14) Focusing on his missionary vocation, another documentary premiered in 2019, _The Field Afar: The Life of Father Vincent Capodanno_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-15) Much of the Guild's documentation was presented in the 2018 biography, "Armed with Faith: The Life of Father Vincent R. Capodanno, MM".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-16)

In 2022, a Vatican advisory panel recommended suspending the sainthood cause, evidently concerned that Capodanno's heroism reflected the battlefield more than religion and that his cause was being led by the American military more than the Maryknoll religious order.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-Jones-17) Questions were also raised concerning Capodanno's obedience to his religious superiors.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-Katinas-18) The Capodanno Guild and the current postulator Nicola Gori began working to overcome the objections,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-Jones-17)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-19) and the Guild's chairman reported that Archbishop Broglio was appointing a three-member historical commission to document Capodanno's pre-military life and spirituality in greater detail.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-20) The commission submitted their report in May 2024. It was reported in April 2026 that the Military Archdiocese expected a decision from the Dicastery in May 2026.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-Katinas-18)

### Medal of Honor citation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Medal of Honor citation")]

Awarded January 7, 1969, Father Capodanno's Medal of Honor citation is as follows:

The [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") in the name of [The Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") takes pride in presenting the MEDAL OF HONOR posthumously to

LIEUTENANT VINCENT R. CAPODANNO  
CHAPLAIN CORPS  
UNITED STATES NAVAL RESERVE

for service as set forth in the following

CITATION:

> For conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty as Chaplain of the 3d Battalion, 5th Marines, 1st Marine Division (Reinforced), FMF, in connection with operations against enemy forces in Quang Tin Province, Republic of Vietnam, on 4 September 1967. In response to reports that the 2d Platoon of M Company was in danger of being overrun by a massed enemy assaulting force, Lieutenant Capodanno left the relative safety of the Company Command Post and ran through an open area raked with fire, directly to the beleaguered platoon. Disregarding the intense enemy small-arms, automatic-weapons, and mortar fire, he moved about the battlefield administering last rites to the dying and giving medical aid to the wounded. When an exploding mortar round inflicted painful multiple wounds to his arms and legs, and severed a portion of his right hand, he steadfastly refused all medical aid. Instead, he directed the corpsmen to help their wounded comrades and, with calm vigor, continued to move about the battlefield as he provided encouragement by voice and example to the valiant Marines. Upon encountering a wounded corpsman in the direct line of fire of an enemy machine gunner positioned approximately fifteen yards away, Lieutenant Capodanno rushed forward in a daring attempt to aid and assist the mortally wounded corpsman. At that instant, only inches from his goal, he was struck down by a burst of machine gun fire. By his heroic conduct on the battlefield, and his inspiring example, Lieutenant Capodanno upheld the finest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life in the cause of freedom.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-21)

/S/ [LYNDON B. JOHNSON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LBJ "LBJ")

### New York City honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: New York City honors")]

In March 1971, the [Knights of Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_of_Columbus "Knights of Columbus"), Madonna Council in Staten Island began a public campaign for a permanent memorial honoring Capodanno in his home borough. In October 1974, a bill was proposed to change the name of Seaside Boulevard to [Father Capodanno Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Capodanno_Boulevard "Father Capodanno Boulevard"); a year later, the bill was passed by the Mayor of New York. For the [United States Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bicentennial "United States Bicentennial") weekend, the city of New York declared July 3, 1976, "Father Capodanno Day", and a memorial Mass was followed by a parade that included the United States Marine Corps Color Guard, marching bands, [Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America") and [Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl_Scouts_of_the_USA "Girl Scouts of the USA") Scouts, and many other groups.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-CatholicMil-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-23)

Near the midpoint of Staten Island's Father Capodanno Boulevard, at the corner of Sand Lane, a monument in the chaplain's honor is made of light gray Barre granite, stands 8' high and 4' wide (2.4m x 1.2m) and has a bronze plaque. Near the north end of the boulevard, alongside [Fort Wadsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Wadsworth "Fort Wadsworth")'s Father Capodanno Memorial Chapel, stands a 1977 statue of the chaplain praying for a fallen corpsman during their final battle.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ModeMemorials-24) The nearby [South Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Beach,_Staten_Island "South Beach, Staten Island") neighborhood is the location of Father Vincent Capodanno Catholic Academy, formed by the merger of two parish elementary schools in 2020.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-25)

### Saint Vincent Chapel, Taiwan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Saint Vincent Chapel, Taiwan")]

Saint Vincent Chapel, in Father Capodanno's Taiwanese mission territory, was his family's first choice as a memorial. Within four months after his death in 1967, almost $4,000 (equivalent to $40,000 in 2025) had been raised by organizations such as [The American Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_American_Legion "The American Legion"), The [Veterans of Foreign Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_of_Foreign_Wars "Veterans of Foreign Wars"), the Knights of Columbus, and the [Marine Corps League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Corps_League "Marine Corps League"). After various delays, the chapel was completed in 1993–1995. It was built in the small mountain town of Thiankou with the help of Father Daniel Dolan, another Maryknoller and Capodanno's former pastor in Taiwan.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-CatholicMil-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ModeMemorials-24)

### Capodanno Hall, San Francisco

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_R._Capodanno&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Capodanno Hall, San Francisco")]

The San Francisco Bay Naval Shipyard ([Hunters Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunters_Point_Naval_Shipyard "Hunters Point Naval Shipyard"), 1941–1994) dedicated Capodanno Hall on November 3, 1969. The hall served as a Bachelor Officers' Quarters. Philip Capodanno unveiled the plaque that describes his brother's heroic deed:[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-CatholicMil-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_R._Capodanno#cite_note-ModeMemorials-24)

> Lieutenant Capodanno made the ultimate sacrifice ministering to the wounded and dying during savage fighting in Vietnam. He has become the third chaplain in our country's history to receive the Medal of Honor and the second Navy chaplain to be so honored.

# 3 Inspiring Books About Catholic Heroes

September 23, 2025

![Image 5: Catholic Heroes Book Club post banner.](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Catholic-Heroes-Book-Club-post-banner-300x150.jpg)

![Image 6: Catholic Heroes Book Club post banner.](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Catholic-Heroes-Book-Club-post-banner.jpg)

Throughout history, Catholic heroism has taken many forms; St. Joan of Arc led troops to victory at just 19 years old; Father John Gerard, SJ, risked his life to minister in a time of persecution; and martyrs like U.S. Navy Chaplain Father Vincent Capodanno, MM, willingly gave their lives for others. Each of them served God in a different way – and each was willing to answer God’s call in their life.

In the latest Basilica Book Club installment, we invite you to discover three books that tell the incredible stories of Catholic heroes across the ages.

### [![Image 7](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Joan-of-Arc_Mark-Twain_book-cover.jpg)](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/joan-of-arc-0906-ja-p)Joan of Arc

Though most readers know Mark Twain for his fiction, few people know that he also wrote a biography of St. Joan of Arc, which he considered his most important work. Meticulously written, the book is the culmination of 12 years of research, including Twain’s extensive archival work in France. After studying detailed accounts by both the French and the English, he made several attempts at drafting the manuscript before he was able to satisfactorily complete it. The result is a remarkably accurate biography of the life and mission of St. Joan of Arc, told by one of America’s greatest storytellers.

[Buy now](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/joan-of-arc-0906-ja-p)

### [![Image 8: Autobiography of a Hunted Priest Book Cover](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Autobiography-of-a-Hunted-Priest-Book-Cover.jpg)](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/the-autobiography-of-a-hunted-priest-john-gerard-0906-ahup-p)The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest

Written by Father John Gerard, SJ, this autobiography tells the story of a Jesuit priest who lived at a time when simply serving his vocation was considered an act of treason. Amidst the brutal persecution of Elizabethan England, Fr. Gerard stopped at nothing to carry out his ministry. In _The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest_, learn how Fr. Gerard snuck onto a Norfolk beach following his ordination, disguised himself as a gentleman, and traveled about the country preaching and ministering to the faithful in secret – always in constant danger. The houses in which he found shelter were frequently raided by “priest hunters”; hide-outs and hair-breadth escapes were part of his daily life. He was ultimately caught, imprisoned, and later moved to the infamous Tower of London where he was brutally tortured. The stirring account of his escape, by means of a rope thrown across the moat, is a daring and magnificent climax to a true story. Here is an accurate and compelling picture of England at a time when Catholics were denied the freedom to worship. Penned over three centuries ago, _The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest_ epitomizes the constant struggle of all human beings through the ages to maintain their freedom.

[Buy now](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/the-autobiography-of-a-hunted-priest-john-gerard-0906-ahup-p)

[![Image 9](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/The-Life-of-Father-Vincent-R.-Capodanno-MM_DiGiovanni_book-cover.jpg)](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/armed-with-faith-the-life-of-fr-vincent-capodanno-1922-9781983237171)

### Armed with Faith: The Life of Father Vincent Capodanno, MM

Amidst the bloodshed and political rancor of the Vietnam War, Father Vincent R. Capodanno stands as a shining example of selfless service. Whether he was serving as a missionary in the Taiwanese mountains, a high school teacher in Hong Kong, or as a chaplain in the United States Navy, he never hesitated to answer God’s call in his life. Politics and personal ambition had no sway for Fr. Capodanno; rather, he was driven by the desire to bring Christ to Marines on the battlefield, providing encouragement in a place of fear and despair. In this gripping biography, learn how he served God across the world, culminating in the battle of September 4, 1976, where he gave up his life to save another.

[Buy now](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/armed-with-faith-the-life-of-fr-vincent-capodanno-1922-9781983237171)

# 3 Inspiring Books About Catholic Heroes

September 23, 2025

![Image 5: Catholic Heroes Book Club post banner.](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Catholic-Heroes-Book-Club-post-banner-300x150.jpg)

![Image 6: Catholic Heroes Book Club post banner.](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Catholic-Heroes-Book-Club-post-banner.jpg)

Throughout history, Catholic heroism has taken many forms; St. Joan of Arc led troops to victory at just 19 years old; Father John Gerard, SJ, risked his life to minister in a time of persecution; and martyrs like U.S. Navy Chaplain Father Vincent Capodanno, MM, willingly gave their lives for others. Each of them served God in a different way – and each was willing to answer God’s call in their life.

In the latest Basilica Book Club installment, we invite you to discover three books that tell the incredible stories of Catholic heroes across the ages.

### [![Image 7](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Joan-of-Arc_Mark-Twain_book-cover.jpg)](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/joan-of-arc-0906-ja-p)Joan of Arc

Though most readers know Mark Twain for his fiction, few people know that he also wrote a biography of St. Joan of Arc, which he considered his most important work. Meticulously written, the book is the culmination of 12 years of research, including Twain’s extensive archival work in France. After studying detailed accounts by both the French and the English, he made several attempts at drafting the manuscript before he was able to satisfactorily complete it. The result is a remarkably accurate biography of the life and mission of St. Joan of Arc, told by one of America’s greatest storytellers.

[Buy now](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/joan-of-arc-0906-ja-p)

### [![Image 8: Autobiography of a Hunted Priest Book Cover](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/Autobiography-of-a-Hunted-Priest-Book-Cover.jpg)](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/the-autobiography-of-a-hunted-priest-john-gerard-0906-ahup-p)The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest

Written by Father John Gerard, SJ, this autobiography tells the story of a Jesuit priest who lived at a time when simply serving his vocation was considered an act of treason. Amidst the brutal persecution of Elizabethan England, Fr. Gerard stopped at nothing to carry out his ministry. In _The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest_, learn how Fr. Gerard snuck onto a Norfolk beach following his ordination, disguised himself as a gentleman, and traveled about the country preaching and ministering to the faithful in secret – always in constant danger. The houses in which he found shelter were frequently raided by “priest hunters”; hide-outs and hair-breadth escapes were part of his daily life. He was ultimately caught, imprisoned, and later moved to the infamous Tower of London where he was brutally tortured. The stirring account of his escape, by means of a rope thrown across the moat, is a daring and magnificent climax to a true story. Here is an accurate and compelling picture of England at a time when Catholics were denied the freedom to worship. Penned over three centuries ago, _The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest_ epitomizes the constant struggle of all human beings through the ages to maintain their freedom.

[Buy now](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/the-autobiography-of-a-hunted-priest-john-gerard-0906-ahup-p)

[![Image 9](https://www.nationalshrine.org/wp-content/uploads/The-Life-of-Father-Vincent-R.-Capodanno-MM_DiGiovanni_book-cover.jpg)](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/armed-with-faith-the-life-of-fr-vincent-capodanno-1922-9781983237171)

### Armed with Faith: The Life of Father Vincent Capodanno, MM

Amidst the bloodshed and political rancor of the Vietnam War, Father Vincent R. Capodanno stands as a shining example of selfless service. Whether he was serving as a missionary in the Taiwanese mountains, a high school teacher in Hong Kong, or as a chaplain in the United States Navy, he never hesitated to answer God’s call in his life. Politics and personal ambition had no sway for Fr. Capodanno; rather, he was driven by the desire to bring Christ to Marines on the battlefield, providing encouragement in a place of fear and despair. In this gripping biography, learn how he served God across the world, culminating in the battle of September 4, 1976, where he gave up his life to save another.

[Buy now](https://www.nationalshrineshops.com/armed-with-faith-the-life-of-fr-vincent-capodanno-1922-9781983237171)

“Chaplain (Lt.) Vincent R. Capodanno, 37, of New York City, wears no physical weapon of war. HIS ARMAMENT is faith – a basic, necessary and treasured attribute to the men around him.”

In the midst of the bloodshed and political rancor of the Vietnam War, the example of Servant of God, Father Vincent R. Capodanno, MM (1929-1967), stands out, for he was motivated neither by politics, nor by personal ambition, nor by military necessity. His was the dedication of Christ’s priest to the Roman Catholic Church and to others, whether as a Maryknoll missionary in the mountains of Taiwan, as a high school teacher in Hong Kong, or as a chaplain in the United States armed forces to men on the battlefield, dying to self to bring Christ to his Marines. In their fear, despair and loneliness in the military camps, and in the mud and filth of the battlefield front lines, Father Capodanno was there, even to the point of perfectly imitating Christ by his personal self-sacrifice to save a man in the heat of battle in Vietnam on September 4, 1967. This is his story.

“No one could risk his life and ultimately be killed to meet the spiritual needs of the Marines if he or she did not believe in the promise of the Kingdom. Father Capodanno brought those unique gifts of the sacraments under fire, because his first concern was to dwell in the house of God forever. You and I want his life and death known, because we believe his example will invite others to stay awake, prepare for the day of the Lord, and be men and women for others. The celebration of the greatness of a figure gone before us is implicitly an invitation to imitate the virtues of that individual. Father Capodanno teaches us the value of commitment and belief. He invites us to give our all in the pursuit of our vocation which is the path the Lord has set for us to share in the joy of His Kingdom.”

-- His Excellency, the Most Reverend Timothy P. Broglio, J.C.D., Archbishop for the Military Services, USA, on the 50th anniversary of the death of Father Vincent R. Capodanno, MM, September 5, 2017

“Chaplain (Lt.) Vincent R. Capodanno, 37, of New York City, wears no physical weapon of war. HIS ARMAMENT is faith – a basic, necessary and treasured attribute to the men around him.”

In the midst of the bloodshed and political rancor of the Vietnam War, the example of Servant of God, Father Vincent R. Capodanno, MM (1929-1967), stands out, for he was motivated neither by politics, nor by personal ambition, nor by military necessity. His was the dedication of Christ’s priest to the Roman Catholic Church and to others, whether as a Maryknoll missionary in the mountains of Taiwan, as a high school teacher in Hong Kong, or as a chaplain in the United States armed forces to men on the battlefield, dying to self to bring Christ to his Marines. In their fear, despair and loneliness in the military camps, and in the mud and filth of the battlefield front lines, Father Capodanno was there, even to the point of perfectly imitating Christ by his personal self-sacrifice to save a man in the heat of battle in Vietnam on September 4, 1967. This is his story.

“No one could risk his life and ultimately be killed to meet the spiritual needs of the Marines if he or she did not believe in the promise of the Kingdom. Father Capodanno brought those unique gifts of the sacraments under fire, because his first concern was to dwell in the house of God forever. You and I want his life and death known, because we believe his example will invite others to stay awake, prepare for the day of the Lord, and be men and women for others. The celebration of the greatness of a figure gone before us is implicitly an invitation to imitate the virtues of that individual. Father Capodanno teaches us the value of commitment and belief. He invites us to give our all in the pursuit of our vocation which is the path the Lord has set for us to share in the joy of His Kingdom.”

-- His Excellency, the Most Reverend Timothy P. Broglio, J.C.D., Archbishop for the Military Services, USA, on the 50th anniversary of the death of Father Vincent R. Capodanno, MM, September 5, 2017

The book “*Armed with Faith: The Life of Father Vincent R. Capodanno, MM*” – which tells the story of a Vietnam‑war chaplain who later became an ordained priest and served public‑service roles in the Navy – was published by **Independently Published**【80】【81】.
